questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response
questions.text: Establishing an overall audit strategy at the beginning of an engagement serves to

answers.text: Set the scope, timing, and direction of the audit and guide the development of the more detailed engagement plan
Provide a fixed, unchangeable schedule of procedures to be completed before the audit report is issued
Document the specific account balances the auditor plans to confirm and the sample sizes for each area
Satisfy the legal requirement that all audit procedures be disclosed to management before field work begins

explanations.a: AU-C Section 300 requires the auditor to establish an overall audit strategy that sets the scope, timing, and direction of the audit and guides the development of the audit plan. The strategy addresses the characteristics of the engagement (entity size, industry, reporting requirements), the reporting objectives (form and timing of reports), the significant factors that determine the engagement team's focus, the results of preliminary engagement activities, and the nature, timing, and extent of resources the firm expects to deploy.
explanations.b: The overall audit strategy is not a fixed, unchangeable schedule. AU-C 300 explicitly acknowledges that the strategy and audit plan may need to be updated as the engagement progresses and new information is obtained — for example, if unexpected significant risks or control deficiencies are identified during testing.
explanations.c: Documenting specific account confirmations and sample sizes is the level of detail found in the engagement plan — not the overall strategy. The strategy operates at a higher level, setting the scope and direction rather than specifying individual procedures for individual accounts.
explanations.d: There is no legal requirement to disclose all planned audit procedures to management before field work begins. In fact, disclosing the details of specific planned procedures (such as which accounts will be confirmed and which will be tested by other means) could undermine the effectiveness of surprise or unpredictable procedures.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response
questions.text: During preliminary planning for a manufacturing company's audit, the auditor learns the entity completed a major acquisition during the year, adding a new business line with different accounting systems and separate internal controls. How does this information MOST affect the overall audit strategy?

answers.text: It has no effect on the strategy since acquisitions are disclosed in the footnotes and are not a primary audit risk
It reduces the audit scope because the acquired entity will be separately audited by another firm

It increases audit complexity and risk — the strategy should expand scope to include procedures specific to the acquired business, its accounting systems, and the accounting treatment of the acquisition itself
It requires the auditor to immediately resign and allow a firm specializing in mergers and acquisitions to lead the engagement

explanations.a: A significant acquisition is one of the most audit-relevant events an entity can experience during the year. It introduces new business risks, potentially new significant accounts, new control environments, and complex accounting issues (purchase price allocation, goodwill, fair value measurements) — all of which increase the risk of material misstatement and require expanded audit attention.
explanations.b: Unless there is a formal component auditor arrangement where another firm separately audits the acquired entity, the principal auditor remains responsible for the consolidated financial statements. Even if a component auditor is used, the overall strategy must address how the principal auditor will oversee and integrate the component audit.
explanations.c: A significant acquisition fundamentally changes the engagement. The auditor must expand the overall strategy to: assess new risks introduced by the acquired business; plan for understanding and testing the acquired entity's accounting systems and internal controls; address the accounting for the acquisition (purchase price allocation, contingent consideration, goodwill impairment testing if applicable); and consider whether specialists are needed to evaluate complex fair value measurements.
explanations.d: Resignation is not an appropriate or required response to a client's acquisition. CPA firms regularly audit entities that have completed acquisitions — the auditor adjusts the scope and approach to address the new complexity, rather than withdrawing.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response
questions.text: Which of the following decisions is BEST characterized as part of the overall audit strategy rather than the more detailed engagement plan?

answers.text: The specific customers selected for accounts receivable confirmation and the monetary threshold below which alternative procedures will be applied
The determination that the audit will rely primarily on substantive analytical procedures rather than tests of controls in areas where the assessed control environment is weak
The identification of which accounting estimates will require the use of an external specialist
The specific document inspection procedures to be applied to a sample of revenue transactions

explanations.a: Identifying specific customers for confirmation and setting monetary thresholds are detailed procedure-level decisions that belong in the engagement plan — they require risk assessment results and audit program detail that goes beyond the scope of the overall strategy.
explanations.b: The decision to rely on substantive analytical procedures rather than tests of controls for areas with weak control environments is a strategic-level decision. The overall strategy determines the general approach — for example, whether the audit will be primarily controls-reliance based (tests of controls followed by reduced substantive procedures) or primarily substantive (direct testing of financial statement assertions with little or no reliance on controls). This direction-setting decision flows into the engagement plan, which specifies the actual procedures.
explanations.c: Identifying specific accounting estimates and deciding to engage specialists for particular estimates is a detailed planning decision that belongs in the engagement plan, once specific risk areas have been identified through risk assessment procedures.
explanations.d: Specific document inspection procedures for revenue transactions are at the level of individual audit program steps — detailed decisions within the engagement plan, not the higher-level overall strategy.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response
questions.text: A specialty retailer faces mounting competitive pressure from online alternatives, narrowing margins, and several industry peers that recently filed for bankruptcy. In developing the overall audit strategy, how should the auditor MOST appropriately respond to this external environment?

answers.text: The external competitive environment is management's concern — the overall strategy should remain unchanged and focus on verifying reported account balances
The auditor should withdraw from the engagement since a potentially failing industry creates unacceptable audit risk
The strategy should emphasize payroll procedures, since retailers in competitive industries tend to understate labor costs

The strategy should direct increased audit attention to inventory valuation, asset impairment, going concern assessment, and revenue recognition — areas most likely to be affected by the competitive pressures and associated management pressure to present favorable results

explanations.a: External industry conditions are a significant input to the overall audit strategy. An industry under severe competitive pressure creates elevated risks of misstatement in specific financial statement areas — particularly inventory (potential overstatement to avoid write-downs), asset impairment (delayed recognition of declining asset values), going concern (risk that management does not disclose or assess going concern properly), and revenue (pressure to recognize revenue aggressively). Ignoring these risks in the strategy would be a failure of planning.
explanations.b: Industry competitive pressure does not require auditor withdrawal — it requires appropriate risk assessment and responsive planning. The auditor's role is most needed precisely when an entity faces significant business challenges, as these environments create the conditions under which material misstatements are most likely.
explanations.c: While labor costs are a significant expense for retailers, the most significant risks from industry competitive pressure relate to inventory valuation, asset impairment, going concern, and revenue recognition — not payroll. Payroll fraud risk is not particularly heightened by competitive industry conditions.
explanations.d: A challenging competitive environment with declining industry performance creates elevated incentives for management to present favorable financial results, which increases fraud risk and the risk of aggressive accounting. The overall strategy should acknowledge these elevated risks and direct resources and emphasis to the financial statement areas most affected by the operating environment — particularly those requiring significant estimates and judgments.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response
questions.text: After the overall audit strategy is established and field work is underway, the auditor discovers that the entity restated a prior-year financial statement due to a previously undetected error in revenue recognition. How should the auditor respond to this discovery?

answers.text: No response is required — prior-year restatements are management's responsibility and do not affect the current-year audit strategy

Revise the overall audit strategy and engagement plan to reflect the increased assessed risk, and perform additional procedures responsive to the heightened risk of misstatement in revenue recognition
Issue a preliminary audit opinion on the restatement before concluding the current-year audit
Resign from the engagement because the restatement indicates management lacks integrity and cannot be trusted

explanations.a: A prior-year restatement is highly relevant to the current-year audit. It indicates that the prior control environment and financial reporting process failed to prevent or detect a material misstatement — which is a significant signal about the quality of the entity's controls and reporting processes. AU-C 300 explicitly recognizes that the strategy and plan may need to be updated based on new information obtained during the audit.
explanations.b: A prior-year restatement — particularly in revenue recognition — is a direct indicator of elevated risk in the current year. The auditor should: (1) reassess the risk of material misstatement in revenue recognition and related accounts; (2) consider whether the control failures that produced the prior error have been remediated; (3) expand substantive testing in the affected areas; and (4) apply heightened professional skepticism to management's current-year revenue recognition judgments. The strategy and plan should be updated to reflect this information.
explanations.c: A preliminary audit opinion on the restatement is not part of the current-year audit engagement. The restatement is management's responsibility; the auditor's role is to consider its implications for current-year risk assessment and to plan appropriate responses.
explanations.d: A restatement does not automatically indicate that management lacks integrity — it may reflect a complex accounting issue, a change in guidance, or an honest error. Resignation is warranted only if there is evidence that management cannot be trusted to provide truthful representations, not merely because a prior error was identified and restated.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response
questions.text: The audit engagement plan is BEST described as

answers.text: A document required by the SEC to be filed along with the issuer's annual report on Form 10-K
A summary of the entity's internal controls that management prepares for the auditor's use
A more detailed document than the overall strategy that specifies the nature, timing, and extent of audit procedures to be performed in each area, responsive to identified risks
The auditor's final report summarizing the conclusions reached for each financial statement assertion

explanations.a: The audit engagement plan is an internal planning document for the auditor's use — it is not filed with the SEC or made available to regulators or the public as part of the entity's annual reporting obligations.
explanations.b: The entity's description of its internal controls is management's documentation — it is not the audit engagement plan. The audit engagement plan is developed by the audit team and documents the auditor's planned procedures.
explanations.c: AU-C Section 300 distinguishes the audit plan from the overall strategy: while the strategy sets the scope and direction, the engagement plan (also called the audit program) translates that strategy into specific, documented procedures. The plan specifies the nature of procedures (e.g., confirmation, inspection, recalculation), their timing (interim vs. year-end), and their extent (sample sizes, coverage percentages) for each significant account and assertion — all designed to respond to the specific risks of material misstatement identified during risk assessment.
explanations.d: The auditor's conclusions are documented in the working papers and communicated in the audit report — not in the engagement plan. The engagement plan is a prospective document describing what procedures will be done, not a retrospective summary of what conclusions were reached.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response
questions.text: Which of the following would MOST likely appear in the engagement plan but NOT in the overall audit strategy?

answers.text: Specific confirmation procedures for accounts receivable — including the identity of customers to be confirmed, the dollar threshold, and alternative procedures for non-responses
The decision to assign a senior manager with manufacturing industry experience as the in-charge on the engagement
The conclusion that the audit will be a controls-reliance approach in accounts payable and a purely substantive approach in revenue
The identification of inventory valuation as a significant audit risk requiring special consideration

explanations.a: Specific confirmation procedures — which customers to confirm, what dollar threshold triggers confirmation versus alternative procedures, and how non-responses will be handled — are detailed audit program steps that belong in the engagement plan. These are procedure-level decisions made after risk assessment is complete, not high-level directional decisions that belong in the strategy.
explanations.b: Staffing decisions — such as assigning a manager with specific industry expertise — are part of the overall strategy's consideration of how to deploy resources effectively. The strategy addresses what expertise is needed and how resources will be allocated, while the engagement plan translates that into specific procedures.
explanations.c: The decision about whether to use a controls-reliance or substantive approach in a given area is a strategic-level decision that drives the overall audit approach. This direction-setting decision belongs in the strategy and then gets implemented in the engagement plan through specific control tests or substantive procedures.
explanations.d: Identifying significant audit risks requiring special audit consideration is part of the risk assessment process and is reflected in the overall strategy. The engagement plan then translates the identified significant risks into specific planned procedures — but the identification itself occurs at the strategy level.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response
questions.text: During testing of a client's revenue transactions, an auditor discovers a significant related-party transaction that was not identified during preliminary risk assessment. The auditor's MOST appropriate response regarding the engagement plan is to

answers.text: Complete all planned procedures first before addressing the newly identified information, to avoid disrupting the original plan
Document the discovery but defer any plan modifications until the following year's audit, when more complete information will be available
Issue a preliminary adverse opinion due to the late discovery of related-party transactions
Update the engagement plan to include additional procedures designed to address the newly identified related-party risk, and consider whether the overall strategy also needs revision

explanations.a: Completing all originally planned procedures before addressing newly discovered information would create a significant risk that the audit fails to respond adequately to the new risk. AU-C 300 anticipates that plans will be updated — the purpose of planning is to create a responsive audit, not to rigidly execute a predetermined program regardless of new information.
explanations.b: Deferring action on a significant newly discovered risk to a future year's audit is not appropriate. If the related-party transaction is material to the current-year financial statements, procedures responsive to that risk must be performed in the current engagement. Deferred discovery is not a cure for current-year audit risk.
explanations.c: A preliminary adverse opinion is not triggered by the late discovery of related-party transactions alone. An adverse opinion would be issued only if the auditor determines that the financial statements are materially misstated — that determination requires additional procedures and evidence, not an immediate opinion based on discovery alone.
explanations.d: AU-C 300 explicitly requires the auditor to update the audit plan when new information becomes available that requires modification of planned procedures. The discovery of a previously unidentified significant related-party transaction warrants: (1) designing additional procedures to understand the nature, terms, and business purpose of the transaction; (2) assessing whether the transaction has been properly disclosed and measured; and (3) considering whether the overall strategy requires revision based on the revised risk assessment.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response
questions.text: In planning the audit of a financial services company, the auditor identifies that the valuation of complex structured financial instruments is a significant risk. When developing the engagement plan's procedures for this risk, the auditor should

answers.text: Design procedures specifically responsive to the significant risk — such as engaging a valuation specialist, obtaining independent pricing from external sources, and applying heightened skepticism to management's assumptions and models
Assign the valuation area to the least experienced team member, since it requires only basic recalculation skills
Reduce testing of other accounts to allow additional time for discussing the valuation with management
Accept management's valuation without independent verification since fair value measurements are inherently subjective and not subject to meaningful audit challenge

explanations.a: AU-C 330 and AU-C 540 require that significant risks — those requiring special audit consideration — have specifically designed responsive procedures that go beyond the standard procedures applied to lower-risk areas. For complex financial instrument valuations, this typically includes: engaging a valuation specialist (AU-C 620) who can independently assess the methodology and key assumptions; obtaining independent pricing from third-party pricing services or market data; testing the significant assumptions (discount rates, volatility, credit spreads) for reasonableness; and reviewing management's valuation models for mathematical accuracy and conceptual soundness.
explanations.b: Assigning the most complex and highest-risk area to the least experienced team member is the opposite of appropriate risk-responsive planning. Significant risks require assignment to audit team members with the experience, expertise, and professional skepticism to design and execute procedures capable of detecting misstatement.
explanations.c: Reducing testing in other areas to allocate time for discussions with management about valuation does not constitute an adequate response to a significant risk. Discussions with management are useful background but are not sufficient audit evidence for complex fair value measurements — independent testing and specialist involvement are required.
explanations.d: Fair value measurements are subject to meaningful audit challenge. The auditor has both the right and the professional obligation to evaluate the reasonableness of management's fair value estimates, even when judgment is involved. AU-C 540 specifically addresses auditing accounting estimates and requires the auditor to evaluate whether management's assumptions are reasonable and whether the valuation model and methodology are appropriate.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response
questions.text: An auditor identifies a high risk of material misstatement in revenue recognition for a software company with complex multi-element arrangements. When translating this risk assessment into the engagement plan, the auditor should

answers.text: Accept management's revenue recognition policy as reasonable because the FASB's ASC 606 guidance was specifically designed to address multi-element arrangements and management would not depart from it
Request that management revise its revenue recognition policy to one that the auditor can more easily test
Identify revenue recognition as a significant risk in the documentation but rely solely on management's representations for this area since it involves significant judgment

Develop specific substantive procedures responsive to the risk — such as detailed contract review, testing of the identification and allocation of performance obligations, and inspection of customer acceptance documentation — in addition to any planned tests of controls

explanations.a: The existence of authoritative guidance (ASC 606) does not eliminate the need for substantive testing — it defines the standard management should apply. The auditor must test whether management has actually applied the standard correctly to specific contracts, particularly when the arrangements involve complex performance obligation identification and transaction price allocation decisions.
explanations.b: The auditor does not have authority to direct management to change its accounting policies to facilitate easier testing. The auditor evaluates whether the policy is appropriate under the applicable framework and whether it has been correctly applied — not whether it is easy to audit.
explanations.c: Management's representations are explicitly insufficient as the primary evidence for areas of significant risk. AU-C 330 requires substantive procedures for all significant risks, and representations alone do not constitute sufficient appropriate audit evidence for a complex, judgment-intensive area like multi-element software revenue recognition.
explanations.d: Significant risks — as defined in AU-C 315 — require specifically designed responsive procedures. For complex revenue arrangements, this means: reviewing a sample of contracts to evaluate management's identification of performance obligations; testing the transaction price allocation among performance obligations using the standalone selling price (or estimation method) specified by ASC 606; inspecting evidence of performance obligation satisfaction (e.g., delivery records, customer acceptance documentation); and assessing the reasonableness of management's judgment calls on constrained variable consideration. Reliance on controls alone, without substantive procedures, is not permitted for significant risks.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response
questions.keyword: external factors (industry conditions, economic environment, regulatory requirements)
questions.text: Understanding external factors — such as industry conditions, the economic environment, and regulatory requirements — during audit planning helps the auditor primarily to

answers.text: Prepare the management discussion and analysis (MD&A) section of the entity's annual report
Determine which external auditing firm should serve as the principal auditor for the engagement
Set the audit fee at an appropriate level given market conditions and competitive pressures in the audit marketplace
Assess the risks of material misstatement arising from the entity's operating environment and identify financial statement areas warranting heightened audit attention

explanations.a: The MD&A is management's responsibility — the auditor may read it to identify inconsistencies with the audited financial statements, but the auditor's role is not to prepare it. Understanding external factors aids in risk assessment, not in drafting management's disclosures.
explanations.b: Selection of the principal auditor is based on the auditor's expertise, registration, and client relationship — not on the entity's external environment. The external environment affects the risk assessment for the audit, not the selection of who performs it.
explanations.c: Audit fee setting involves consideration of engagement complexity, risk, staffing requirements, and market factors — but the primary professional purpose of understanding external factors during planning is risk assessment, not commercial fee negotiation.
explanations.d: AU-C Section 315 requires the auditor to obtain an understanding of the entity and its environment — including external factors — as part of risk assessment procedures. External factors such as industry conditions (competitive pressures, cyclicality, margin trends), the economic environment (interest rates, credit conditions, GDP trends), and the regulatory environment (recent rule changes, enforcement actions) all influence the risks that the entity faces and consequently the risk of material misstatement in specific financial statement areas.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response
questions.keyword: external factors (industry conditions, economic environment, regulatory requirements)
questions.text: A bank holding company is audited during a period of sharply rising interest rates that has reduced the fair values of its fixed-rate loan portfolio and increased prepayment risk on its mortgage-backed securities. How does this external factor MOST affect audit planning?

answers.text: It increases the risk of material misstatement in fair value measurements of investment securities and interest income recognition — the auditor should plan for additional scrutiny of these areas and consider whether specialist involvement is needed
Interest rate changes are disclosed in the market risk footnote and are management's responsibility — the auditor does not need to plan additional procedures
The risk impact is mitigated by the bank's loan origination activities, which benefit from rising rates, so no additional audit procedures are needed
The auditor should expand payroll testing because rising rates cause banks to hire more compliance staff

explanations.a: Sharply rising interest rates create direct financial statement risks for a bank holding company: (1) fair values of fixed-rate debt securities decline as rates rise — the auditor must assess whether management's fair value measurements (and any impairment conclusions for held-to-maturity securities) are appropriate; (2) prepayment risk on mortgage-backed securities affects the projected cash flows used in their valuation; (3) the interest rate environment may affect the bank's net interest margin and the adequacy of its credit loss reserves if borrowers are stressed by higher rates. These are areas requiring heightened audit scrutiny and potentially the involvement of a financial instruments valuation specialist.
explanations.b: Interest rate disclosures in footnotes do not eliminate the need for audit procedures on the underlying measurements. The footnote discloses the risk; the auditor must assess whether the amounts reported in the financial statements (fair values, impairments, interest income) are accurately measured given the prevailing rate environment.
explanations.c: While loan origination may benefit from rising rates, this does not offset the audit risks created by declining fair values in the existing fixed-rate portfolio. Audit planning must address specific risk areas — a benefit in one area does not reduce the audit risk in a different, adversely affected area.
explanations.d: There is no established relationship between rising interest rates and expanded payroll testing. Payroll risk is driven by payroll process controls and management override risk — not by the interest rate environment.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response
questions.keyword: external factors (industry conditions, economic environment, regulatory requirements)
questions.text: A healthcare provider is audited shortly after a major regulatory change that significantly reduces Medicare reimbursement rates for the entity's primary service lines. In assessing the risks created by this regulatory change, the auditor should recognize that it

answers.text: Has no audit significance because revenue changes resulting from rate changes are required disclosures and are therefore transparent to financial statement users

Creates heightened risk of misstatement in revenue recognition, accounts receivable collectability, going concern, and asset impairment — and may increase the risk that management faces pressure to present favorable results
Primarily affects only the cash flow statement and has no significant impact on income statement or balance sheet accounts
Requires the auditor to immediately notify CMS (Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services) of the audit engagement

explanations.a: Regulatory rate changes have audit significance beyond their disclosure impact. When revenues are significantly reduced by a regulatory change, it creates the conditions for material misstatement: management may face pressure to overstate revenues or understate costs, delay or avoid recognizing impairments, and may not adequately assess or disclose going concern risks. Disclosure alone does not eliminate the need for auditor attention to the accounting implications.
explanations.b: A significant reduction in Medicare reimbursement rates creates multiple interconnected audit risks: (1) revenue risk — if the entity has not properly reduced its expected net patient service revenue to reflect the new rates, revenue and accounts receivable may be overstated; (2) accounts receivable collectability — the accounts receivable carrying value must reflect the new expected reimbursement rates; (3) going concern — if the rate reduction threatens the entity's financial viability, management must assess and disclose going concern risks; (4) asset impairment — if the entity's long-lived assets or goodwill are no longer recoverable at the reduced revenue levels, impairment may be required. The rate reduction also creates financial pressure that may heighten fraud risk.
explanations.c: Revenue recognition affects the income statement (net patient service revenue) and the balance sheet (accounts receivable, allowance for contractual adjustments) — not just the cash flow statement. The impacts are pervasive across financial statement line items.
explanations.d: Auditors have no obligation to notify CMS of their audit engagement. The auditor's responsibility is to plan and perform the audit appropriately given the changed regulatory environment — not to notify the regulatory agency that issued the rate change.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response
questions.text: Understanding internal factors of an entity during audit planning includes gaining knowledge of which of the following?

answers.text: The personal investment portfolios of the entity's customers and their credit ratings
The resumes and employment histories of audit team members assigned to the engagement
The entity's business operations, ownership and governance structure, accounting policies, and management's philosophy and operating style
The SEC's current enforcement priorities and the volume of recent restatements in the entity's industry

explanations.a: The investment portfolios and credit ratings of the entity's customers may be relevant to understanding credit risk and the collectability of accounts receivable, but they are characteristics of the entity's customers — not internal factors of the entity itself. Internal factors relate to the entity being audited.
explanations.b: Audit team member backgrounds are relevant to the firm's quality control and engagement staffing decisions — they are not internal factors of the audited entity. Internal factors describe characteristics of the entity, not the audit team.
explanations.c: AU-C Section 315 requires the auditor to understand the entity's: business model and operations (products, services, customers, suppliers); ownership and governance structure (who controls the entity, the role of the board and audit committee); management's philosophy and operating style (attitude toward risk, approach to financial reporting); and accounting policies adopted (choices among acceptable alternatives, consistency with industry practices). These internal factors collectively shape the risk of material misstatement.
explanations.d: SEC enforcement priorities and industry restatement patterns are external factors — information about the regulatory environment and industry context — not internal factors of the specific entity being audited.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response
questions.text: An entity is a family-owned company where one individual serves simultaneously as chairman of the board, CEO, and controlling shareholder. In assessing risk during planning, this internal structure is MOST significant because

answers.text: Family-owned companies are exempt from GAAP and may use cash-basis accounting

Concentrated power in one individual increases the risk of management override of controls and may indicate a weak control environment — warranting expanded procedures responsive to this elevated risk
The individual's combined roles guarantee that the entity's financial statements are more reliable, since one person has complete oversight
The structure is only relevant if the entity is planning an initial public offering

explanations.a: Family-owned companies are not exempt from GAAP. The applicable financial reporting framework (e.g., US GAAP or a special purpose framework) applies to all entities regardless of ownership structure. Family ownership does not change the financial reporting requirements.
explanations.b: When one individual holds concentrated decision-making authority — acting as chairman, CEO, and controlling shareholder — the normal checks and balances inherent in a governance structure (independent board oversight, separation of management from ownership) are significantly weakened. This concentration of power is a significant risk factor for management override of controls and for the integrity of the financial reporting process. The auditor should plan procedures specifically responsive to this elevated risk, including careful evaluation of significant management judgments and estimates, and greater attention to unusual or related-party transactions.
explanations.c: A single individual having oversight of all functions does not enhance reliability — it removes the independent checks that make governance effective. Reliable financial reporting generally requires independent oversight and appropriate segregation of authority, not concentration in one person.
explanations.d: Governance structure is a risk factor that affects every year's audit — not only periods preceding an IPO. The concentration of authority creates ongoing elevated risk of management override and control environment weakness in every reporting period.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response
questions.text: For an issuer subject to the Sarbanes-Oxley Act, understanding the audit committee's composition and level of engagement during audit planning is important primarily because

answers.text: An effective, engaged audit committee improves the quality of governance over financial reporting, which is relevant to assessing the overall control environment and management integrity — and an ineffective audit committee is itself a risk factor
The auditor is required to report all audit findings directly to the SEC, bypassing the audit committee entirely
The audit committee's pre-approval of all tax services is required before the auditor can assess revenue risk
The audit committee members are personally liable for misstatements in the financial statements and this exposure ensures accurate reporting

explanations.a: An audit committee that is actively engaged, composed of independent and financially knowledgeable directors, meets regularly with the auditor, and exercises meaningful oversight of financial reporting is a positive governance element that supports the integrity of the reporting process. Conversely, an audit committee that is passive, lacks financial expertise, or fails to exercise independent oversight is itself a risk factor — it reduces the effectiveness of governance as a check on management behavior. The auditor considers audit committee effectiveness as part of the overall assessment of the control environment.
explanations.b: The auditor does not report findings directly to the SEC, bypassing the audit committee. The auditor communicates significant findings to the audit committee (AU-C 260, and for issuers, PCAOB AS 1301). The SEC receives the auditor's public report — not internal audit findings communicated during the engagement.
explanations.c: Audit committee pre-approval of tax services is an SEC independence requirement — it enables tax services to be provided without impairing independence. It is not a prerequisite for the auditor's assessment of revenue risk. Revenue risk assessment is a professional judgment based on the entity's characteristics, accounting policies, and identified fraud risk factors.
explanations.d: Audit committee members have governance responsibilities, but their potential liability does not guarantee accurate financial reporting. The auditor cannot assume that potential liability creates accurate reporting and must conduct an independent assessment of audit risk.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response
questions.text: During planning, an auditor learns that the entity recently converted from cash-basis to accrual-basis accounting in connection with new bank loan requirements. This internal factor is MOST likely to heighten audit risk in which specific areas?

answers.text: Payroll and employee benefits — because the conversion requires recalculation of all historical wages
Property, plant, and equipment — because accrual accounting requires different depreciation calculations than cash-basis
There are no heightened risks — the conversion to accrual accounting is straightforward and well-covered by accounting literature

Revenue recognition, accrued liabilities, and accounts payable — because the conversion requires establishing opening accrual balances through significant judgment, and accounting staff may lack experience with accrual concepts

explanations.a: Payroll and employee benefits are impacted by the conversion to the extent that accrued wages, vacation liability, and pension obligations must be recognized — but these are subsets of the broader accrued liabilities risk. Stating payroll as the primary area understates the scope of the conversion's risk implications.
explanations.b: While depreciation methodology may be affected by the conversion (cash-basis may have expensed certain capital items), the highest-risk areas are those involving significant opening accrual balance determinations where judgment is most required — receivables, payables, and accrued liabilities.
explanations.c: A conversion from cash-basis to accrual-basis accounting involves substantial complexity — particularly in establishing opening balances for items that were not previously tracked: accounts receivable (recognizing revenue earned but not yet collected), accounts payable (recognizing obligations incurred but not yet paid), and accrued liabilities (wages, benefits, interest, and other accruals). This conversion is not straightforward and requires significant judgment.
explanations.d: The conversion from cash to accrual basis creates heightened risk in: (1) revenue recognition — establishing opening accounts receivable requires identifying revenue earned in prior periods that had not been collected; (2) accounts payable — identifying obligations incurred but not paid at the conversion date requires reviewing unpaid vendor invoices and commitments; (3) accrued liabilities — wages earned, vacation accruals, and other accruals must be estimated for the first time. Accounting personnel accustomed to cash-basis recording may lack the experience to correctly apply accrual concepts, increasing the risk of error.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response
questions.text: During planning, an auditor notes three internal factors: (1) management has set aggressive profit targets tied to executive compensation bonuses; (2) the CFO resigned unexpectedly and has been replaced by an external hire who has been in the role for 30 days; and (3) the entity recently expanded into three new international markets with different regulatory and tax environments. Taken together, how should these factors influence the auditor's overall risk assessment?

answers.text: These factors cancel each other out — the new CFO's external perspective compensates for management's aggressive targets and the international expansion
Only the CFO transition is significant — management turnover is the most auditable of the three factors and should receive the most audit attention

These factors collectively indicate elevated fraud risk (incentive from compensation structure, opportunity from CFO transition and new environments), warrant heightened professional skepticism, and suggest that substantive procedures should be expanded in revenue, management estimates, and international operations
The factors are individually minor and only become significant if misstatements are actually detected during testing

explanations.a: Risk factors do not 'cancel out' — they accumulate. A new CFO's external perspective does not compensate for the elevated fraud risk created by aggressive compensation-linked targets and the operational challenges of rapid international expansion. Each factor adds to the risk environment independently.
explanations.b: While the CFO transition is significant, focusing exclusively on management turnover understates the combined risk picture. The fraud risk triangle identifies three conditions that contribute to fraud: incentive/pressure, opportunity, and rationalization. The three identified factors map directly to two of these elements: the compensation structure creates incentive/pressure, and the CFO transition and new international environments create opportunities for misstatement to go undetected.
explanations.c: The three factors collectively create a high-risk environment for the audit. (1) Aggressive compensation-linked targets create financial incentive for management to misstate results — a classic fraud risk indicator. (2) A new CFO with 30 days' experience may not yet have adequate oversight over the entity's financial reporting processes, creating an opportunity for errors or irregularities to go undetected. (3) Rapid international expansion into unfamiliar regulatory environments creates complexity and potential for misapplication of tax, regulatory, and financial reporting requirements. Together, these factors warrant: expanded substantive procedures in revenue and key estimates; heightened professional skepticism when evaluating management's judgments; careful attention to international reporting; and explicit assessment of fraud risk as required by AU-C 240.
explanations.d: Risk assessment is prospective and preventive — the auditor does not wait for misstatements to determine that risk factors are significant. The purpose of risk assessment is to identify conditions that create the risk of misstatement before testing, so that the audit plan can be designed to address those risks.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response
questions.text: The Committee of Sponsoring Organizations (COSO) Internal Control — Integrated Framework identifies which five components of internal control?

answers.text: Authorization, segregation of duties, physical controls, reconciliations, and independent reviews
Control environment, risk assessment, control activities, information and communication, and monitoring activities
Detective controls, preventive controls, corrective controls, directive controls, and compensating controls
Financial reporting, operations, compliance, strategic objectives, and asset safeguarding

explanations.a: Authorization, segregation of duties, physical controls, reconciliations, and independent reviews are examples of specific control activities — one component of the COSO framework — not the five components themselves. These are types of controls within the Control Activities component.
explanations.b: The COSO Internal Control — Integrated Framework (2013) identifies five interconnected components: (1) Control Environment — the foundation that establishes the tone and organizational context; (2) Risk Assessment — management's process for identifying and assessing risks to objectives; (3) Control Activities — policies and procedures that address risks and support the achievement of objectives; (4) Information and Communication — the systems and processes that support the flow of relevant information; and (5) Monitoring Activities — ongoing and separate evaluations to assess whether controls are operating as intended.
explanations.c: Detective, preventive, corrective, directive, and compensating controls are classifications of controls by how they respond to risk — they are not the five COSO components. These classifications describe the mechanism of individual controls, not the framework's organizational structure.
explanations.d: Financial reporting, operations, compliance, and strategic objectives are the four objective categories in the COSO Enterprise Risk Management (ERM) Framework — related to but distinct from the internal control framework. The COSO internal control framework has three objective categories (operations, reporting, compliance) and five components of control.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response
questions.text: The COSO framework specifies that internal control supports achievement of objectives in which three categories?

answers.text: Internal objectives, external objectives, and compliance objectives
Short-term objectives, long-term objectives, and strategic objectives
Financial objectives, non-financial objectives, and tax objectives
Operations objectives, reporting objectives, and compliance objectives

explanations.a: Internal and external objectives are not the COSO objective categories. These terms do not appear in the COSO internal control framework as defined objective categories.
explanations.b: Short-term, long-term, and strategic objectives are planning and management concepts — they do not represent the three COSO objective categories. The COSO framework organizes objectives by their nature and stakeholder, not by time horizon.
explanations.c: Financial, non-financial, and tax objectives are not the COSO objective categories. While financial reporting is a subcategory within reporting objectives, 'financial objectives' is not the framework's terminology.
explanations.d: The COSO Internal Control — Integrated Framework establishes three categories of objectives that internal control supports: (1) Operations objectives — the effectiveness and efficiency of the entity's operations, including safeguarding of assets; (2) Reporting objectives — the reliability of financial and non-financial reporting for internal and external use; and (3) Compliance objectives — adherence to applicable laws and regulations. These three categories are represented in the COSO cube diagram as columns.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response
questions.text: An auditor uses the COSO Internal Control — Integrated Framework as the basis for evaluating an entity's internal control. The primary benefit of using COSO as a reference framework is that it

answers.text: Provides a comprehensive, standardized structure for evaluating each component of internal control — enabling systematic assessment of design adequacy and operating effectiveness across the entire organization
Replaces the need for the auditor to perform tests of controls, since COSO-compliant entities have already assessed their own controls
Guarantees that an entity's financial statements are free of material misstatement when management asserts compliance with COSO
Is the only framework acceptable to the SEC and PCAOB for evaluating internal control over financial reporting

explanations.a: The COSO framework provides a common language and structure for describing, evaluating, and communicating about internal control. By using COSO, auditors can systematically address all five components and 17 principles across the three objective categories — ensuring that the evaluation covers the full scope of what constitutes effective internal control rather than focusing only on transaction-level controls or specific accounts.
explanations.b: The COSO framework is a tool that facilitates internal control evaluation — it does not substitute for audit testing. Management's assessment of its own controls (required under SOX 404(a)) is separate from the auditor's independent evaluation. The auditor must independently test controls to reach conclusions about their effectiveness.
explanations.c: COSO compliance, or management's assertion of COSO compliance, does not guarantee freedom from material misstatement. Internal controls provide reasonable assurance — not absolute assurance — and even well-designed COSO-based controls can fail due to human error, management override, or collusion.
explanations.d: While COSO is the most widely used framework for ICFR evaluation in the US (and is implicitly referenced in SEC and PCAOB guidance), the SEC has not mandated COSO as the exclusive framework. Other suitable frameworks include those issued by recognized standard-setting bodies — COSO is the dominant choice in practice, but the regulations specify that the framework used must be established by a body that follows due process, not specifically that it must be COSO.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response
questions.text: An auditor identifies that the entity's risk assessment process (the COSO Risk Assessment component) does not identify or address IT-related risks — specifically, risks from unauthorized access to systems processing financial data. How does this deficiency in the Risk Assessment component MOST likely affect other COSO components?

answers.text: It has no effect on other components — each COSO component operates independently and failures in one do not cascade to others
It means the Control Environment is also deficient, since risk assessment is a prerequisite for establishing the control environment

It likely means that Control Activities addressing IT access are inadequate or absent, because if management does not identify IT access as a risk, it is unlikely to have designed specific controls to address that risk
It only affects the Monitoring Activities component, which is responsible for detecting deficiencies in risk assessment

explanations.a: The COSO components are interconnected — a deficiency in one component typically cascades to others. The framework explicitly recognizes that the components are interrelated and that a deficiency in one area can affect the effectiveness of the overall system.
explanations.b: While Risk Assessment supports the Control Environment, a failure in risk assessment does not automatically mean the Control Environment itself is deficient. The Control Environment is driven by governance, ethics, and tone at the top — it can be sound even if the risk assessment process is incomplete in certain areas.
explanations.c: The COSO framework is designed so that the Risk Assessment component drives the design of Control Activities. If management's risk assessment process fails to identify IT access as a risk, management is unlikely to have specifically designed and implemented control activities to prevent unauthorized access to financial systems. This creates a gap: the risk exists but no control has been designed to address it. Auditors evaluating the COSO components should expect that deficiencies in Risk Assessment will produce corresponding gaps in Control Activities.
explanations.d: Monitoring Activities assess whether existing controls are operating effectively — they detect failures in controls that have been designed. If a risk was never identified and no control was ever designed for it (because Risk Assessment failed), Monitoring Activities would not detect the absence of a control they were never designed to monitor.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response
questions.text: The control environment is described as the 'foundation' of the COSO framework. In evaluating the control environment, an auditor finds that management has a history of overriding established policies when they find them inconvenient, and that the board of directors has been passive in its oversight role. How should this finding affect the auditor's overall evaluation of internal control?

answers.text: It has limited impact — as long as transaction-level controls are well-designed, a weak control environment can be overlooked

A weak control environment undermines the effectiveness of all other COSO components — even well-designed risk assessment processes, control activities, and monitoring may not function as intended when the tone at the top does not support control compliance
The finding suggests the auditor should expand payroll testing since management override typically occurs in payroll processing
The auditor should qualify the audit opinion solely on the basis of the control environment evaluation, without performing further tests

explanations.a: The control environment cannot be overlooked even when transaction-level controls appear well-designed. COSO specifically identifies the control environment as the foundation because it influences the effectiveness of all other components. A poor control environment means that even well-designed controls may not operate as intended — people follow the tone set by management, not the written policies that management itself overrides.
explanations.b: The COSO framework describes the control environment as the foundation upon which all other components rest. When management routinely overrides policies and the board is passive in oversight, the controls that are formally in place may not actually be followed in practice. This creates a pervasive risk: any specific control activity can be bypassed if management chooses to do so, and monitoring activities may not detect or address exceptions that management sanctions. The auditor must respond by: expanding substantive procedures significantly; applying heightened professional skepticism to all management representations and estimates; specifically assessing fraud risk given the management override history; and focusing particular attention on journal entries and period-end adjustments.
explanations.c: Management override can occur in any financial statement area — not specifically in payroll. The response to a weak control environment should be comprehensive expansion of substantive procedures across significant accounts, not a narrow focus on payroll.
explanations.d: An audit opinion is issued on the financial statements (and ICFR in an integrated audit) — not solely on the control environment evaluation. The auditor must complete sufficient audit procedures to form an opinion on the financial statements and, if applicable, ICFR. An evaluation of the control environment alone is not sufficient basis for issuing any audit opinion.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response
questions.text: An auditor evaluates ICFR across two divisions of a multi-division manufacturer. Division A (60% of revenue) has a strong control environment, effective risk assessment, well-designed control activities, and robust monitoring. Division B (40% of revenue) has a poor control environment, high accounting staff turnover, and ineffective monitoring. In evaluating entity-level ICFR using COSO, which conclusion is MOST appropriate?

answers.text: ICFR is effective because Division A's controls, representing 60% of revenue, are sufficient to conclude that the entity-level system is effective on a weighted-average basis
ICFR should be evaluated separately for each division and two separate ICFR opinions should be issued

The entity-level ICFR evaluation must consider both divisions — Division A's effective controls do not compensate for Division B's control environment failures, which likely constitute significant deficiencies or material weaknesses requiring communication and inclusion in the ICFR opinion
ICFR can be concluded as effective if management remediates Division B's weaknesses within 90 days of the balance sheet date

explanations.a: Internal control effectiveness is not evaluated on a weighted-average basis. A significant deficiency or material weakness in a component representing 40% of revenue is material — it cannot be diluted by averaging with a larger, better-controlled division. If Division B's control environment failures create a reasonable possibility that a material misstatement would not be prevented or detected, a material weakness exists regardless of Division A's performance.
explanations.b: A single ICFR opinion covers the entity as a whole — two separate opinions are not issued for different divisions. The auditor evaluates ICFR at the entity level, which requires assessing all significant components, including both Division A and Division B.
explanations.c: PCAOB AS 2201 requires the auditor to evaluate entity-level ICFR, which encompasses all significant components. Division B's control environment failures — poor tone, high turnover in accounting staff, and ineffective monitoring — represent conditions under which financial misstatements are more likely to occur and less likely to be detected. These conditions likely constitute significant deficiencies or material weaknesses. Strong controls in Division A do not compensate for or override the material control environment failures in Division B — each component must be evaluated on its own merits as a part of the whole.
explanations.d: Post-year-end remediation does not change the ICFR evaluation as of the fiscal year-end. PCAOB AS 2201 evaluates ICFR effectiveness as of the balance sheet date. If material weaknesses or significant deficiencies exist at year-end, they must be reflected in the ICFR opinion regardless of subsequent remediation plans.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response
questions.keyword: control environment, IT general controls, and entity-level controls
questions.text: Entity-level controls differ from transaction-level controls primarily because entity-level controls

answers.text: Have a pervasive effect across the organization — for example, the control environment, centralized monitoring activities, and entity-level IT controls affect the effectiveness of many other controls throughout the entity
Are performed by senior management only and are never delegated to lower-level employees
Address only the completeness assertion for significant financial statement accounts
Are not subject to evaluation in a GAAS audit of a nonissuer entity

explanations.a: Entity-level controls are distinguished by their pervasive effect. Unlike transaction-level controls (which address specific risks within individual processes — for example, three-way matching in accounts payable), entity-level controls operate across the organization and influence the effectiveness of many other controls. Examples include: the overall control environment (tone at the top, ethical culture); entity-level risk assessment processes; centralized monitoring activities (management review of financial results); and IT general controls, which affect the reliability of all application controls that operate in the IT environment.
explanations.b: Entity-level controls are not limited to activities performed by senior management. For example, an ethics hotline accessible to all employees is an entity-level control, as are entity-wide policies and procedures, HR controls over hiring and training, and pervasive IT infrastructure controls.
explanations.c: Entity-level controls do not address only the completeness assertion. They operate across all financial reporting assertions (existence/occurrence, completeness, accuracy, valuation, rights and obligations, presentation and disclosure) through their pervasive influence on the control environment.
explanations.d: Entity-level controls are relevant to all audits — both issuer and nonissuer. Under AU-C 315, the auditor must obtain an understanding of the entity's control environment as part of understanding the entity and its internal control, regardless of whether the audit is of an issuer or nonissuer.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response
questions.keyword: control environment, IT general controls, and entity-level controls
questions.text: IT general controls (ITGCs) are foundational to the reliability of automated application controls. Which statement BEST explains why ITGC weaknesses are so significant in an audit?

answers.text: ITGC weaknesses always require the auditor to disclaim an opinion because the financial statements cannot be audited when IT controls fail
ITGCs only affect the completeness of data and have no bearing on the accuracy of automated calculations within application systems
ITGC weaknesses require immediate regulatory reporting to the PCAOB even when the audit is of a nonissuer entity

If ITGCs are ineffective — particularly controls over access to programs and data and program changes — the auditor cannot rely on automated application controls, because unauthorized changes to programs or data may have undermined those controls throughout the period

explanations.a: ITGC weaknesses do not automatically require a disclaimer of opinion. They require the auditor to expand substantive testing to compensate for the inability to rely on automated controls — but sufficient audit evidence can still be obtained through enhanced substantive procedures.
explanations.b: ITGCs affect all aspects of the IT environment, not just completeness. Program change controls affect whether automated calculations function correctly; access controls affect whether data can be manipulated or extracted without authorization; computer operations controls affect whether processing runs completely and correctly. All assertions are potentially affected.
explanations.c: ITGC weaknesses are communicated to management and those charged with governance through the internal control communication process (AU-C 265 for nonissuers; PCAOB AS 1305 for issuers). They are not reported to the PCAOB as individual audit findings — the PCAOB oversight is conducted through its inspection program, not through individual auditor filings about client control deficiencies.
explanations.d: ITGCs are general controls that govern the overall IT environment in which application controls operate. If program change controls are ineffective, unauthorized changes may have been made to application programs — including the automated controls within those programs — without detection. If access controls are ineffective, unauthorized individuals may have accessed and altered programs or data. In either case, the auditor cannot conclude that automated application controls operated as designed throughout the period, making ITGC effectiveness a prerequisite for relying on those automated controls.
