questions.name: Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response
questions.keyword: control environment, IT general controls, and entity-level controls
questions.text: An auditor discovers that the entity's IT change management controls are ineffective — software updates are deployed to the production environment without formal testing, documentation, or multi-person approval. How does this ITGC deficiency MOST affect the auditor's approach to automated application controls in the revenue recognition system?

answers.text: The ITGC deficiency is immaterial if the revenue system has been operating without reported errors during the current year

The ITGC deficiency means the auditor cannot rely on automated application controls in the revenue system without additional procedures — the auditor should perform detailed review of system changes during the period or significantly expand substantive revenue testing
The auditor should immediately notify the entity's external IT consultant to fix the change management process before continuing the audit
Automated controls in the revenue system remain reliable as long as they were functioning correctly at the beginning of the audit period

explanations.a: The absence of reported errors during the year does not mean the controls are reliable — it means no errors were noticed. Without effective change management controls, unauthorized or untested changes could have been introduced into the revenue system at any point during the year, potentially affecting how automated controls function. The auditor cannot conclude controls are reliable based solely on the absence of detected errors.
explanations.b: Effective IT change management controls provide assurance that only authorized, properly tested changes are made to application programs. Without this assurance, the auditor does not know whether the automated application controls in the revenue system — such as automated approval limits, duplicate payment detection, or revenue cutoff controls — have been altered or compromised. To address this uncertainty, the auditor should either: (1) expand the review of system changes to test whether unauthorized changes were made to revenue-related programs; or (2) forego reliance on automated revenue controls and expand substantive testing of revenue transactions to directly test the revenue assertions.
explanations.c: Notifying the IT consultant to fix the control is a management communication (through the internal control deficiency process) — it is not within the auditor's authority to require and does not cure the audit risk created by the historical absence of effective controls during the audit period.
explanations.d: An IT system's configuration at the beginning of the year can be changed at any point during the year if change management controls are ineffective. There is no assurance that controls functioning correctly at the start of the year continued to function correctly throughout the period if unauthorized or untested changes could have been introduced.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response
questions.keyword: control environment, IT general controls, and entity-level controls
questions.text: Management requires all employees to annually certify compliance with the company's ethics code. However, internal audit reports reveal that ethics violations by senior executives are routinely resolved informally without discipline, while violations by lower-level employees result in termination. How should the auditor evaluate this entity-level control?

answers.text: The ethics certification program is an effective entity-level control because formal certification reduces the likelihood of violations at all levels of the organization
The program is effective as long as violations are resolved — the method of resolution is a management prerogative and is not relevant to the auditor's assessment

The discrepancy between how violations are addressed for executives versus lower-level employees reveals that the ethics program is not operating effectively — the actual tone at the top is inconsistent with the stated code, creating a weak control environment that increases fraud risk
The auditor should report this finding directly to the SEC as a violation of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act

explanations.a: The formal existence of an ethics certification program is a design element — but the operating effectiveness of the control depends on whether it actually deters and addresses violations. When senior executives are exempt from the same consequences applied to lower-level employees, the certification loses its meaning as a behavioral deterrent, making the program operationally ineffective despite its formal existence.
explanations.b: The method of resolving violations is highly relevant because it reveals the actual tone at the top — the real message from leadership about whether ethics are enforced. When senior executives face no consequences for violations, the actual message is that the code does not apply to those with authority. This is the opposite of what the code is designed to achieve.
explanations.c: The COSO framework identifies the control environment as the foundation of internal control, and the control environment is shaped by the actual behavior of leadership — not just the policies that leadership has documented. A dual standard — strict enforcement for employees, informal resolution for executives — reveals a fundamental weakness in the control environment that increases the risk of management override, fraudulent financial reporting, and rationalization of unethical behavior. The auditor should: heighten professional skepticism in all areas involving management judgment; specifically assess fraud risk indicators related to management integrity; and expand substantive procedures.
explanations.d: The auditor does not report internal ethics inconsistencies directly to the SEC as an automatic reporting obligation. Communications about control deficiencies go to management and the audit committee (AU-C 265, PCAOB AS 1305). Reporting to the SEC of potential fraud would be required only under specific circumstances involving illegal acts (AU-C 250) — not for ethics policy administration inconsistencies.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response
questions.keyword: control environment, IT general controls, and entity-level controls
questions.text: An auditor notes: (1) ITGCs are effective — program changes are well-controlled; (2) entity-level monitoring is active — management regularly reviews operational and financial variance reports; (3) however, the CFO approved his own transactions three times during the year, each time exceeding his individual authorization limit, citing 'business urgency.' What is the MOST appropriate overall assessment of the control environment?

answers.text: Controls are effective overall because the strong ITGCs and active monitoring compensate for the three isolated authorization overrides
The three exceptions are minor operational issues that should be communicated to management but do not affect the auditor's reliance on controls

The CFO's self-authorization of transactions above his own limit is a breakdown of the authorization control structure that may rise to a significant deficiency or material weakness, regardless of other controls' effectiveness — and it is a fraud risk indicator requiring heightened skepticism and expanded procedures
The CFO's behavior is excusable because business urgency is a recognized exception to authorization controls under COSO

explanations.a: Strong ITGCs and monitoring do not compensate for a breakdown in the authorization control structure at the CFO level. Effective monitoring is supposed to detect these overrides — yet the overrides occurred three times. This suggests either monitoring failed to detect or report the exceptions, or that the overrides were detected but not addressed, which itself is a control failure. Controls are not evaluated by averaging — a specific breakdown in a specific control must be evaluated on its own merits.
explanations.b: A CFO self-approving transactions above his own authorization limit is not a minor operational issue. Authorization controls exist precisely to prevent individuals from approving transactions in which they have a conflict of interest or from committing funds beyond their authority. Self-authorization by a senior executive — three times in one year — is a significant breakdown that: (1) undermines the integrity of the authorization control; (2) indicates the control is not operating as designed; and (3) creates a fraud risk indicator, since the same pattern of behavior could be used to authorize unauthorized payments or conceal misappropriation.
explanations.c: Authorization controls require that someone with appropriate authority — other than the person initiating the transaction — approves the transaction. When the CFO approves his own transactions above his authorization limit, the fundamental control objective (independent approval) is defeated. Under COSO, this represents a control that is either not properly designed (if self-approval is actually permitted) or not operating effectively (if it is not permitted but occurred without detection or consequence). The recurrence three times in one year elevates this to at least a significant deficiency and potentially a material weakness, requiring: written communication to management and TCWG, expanded fraud-risk responsive procedures, and heightened skepticism for CFO-approved transactions.
explanations.d: 'Business urgency' is not a recognized exception to authorization controls under COSO or under any auditing standard. Authorization controls are designed to function regardless of claimed urgency — proper authorization can be obtained quickly if the governance structure is well-designed. Accepting 'business urgency' as a justification for bypassing controls is itself a control environment weakness.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response
questions.keyword: business processes and internal control design
questions.text: Understanding the entity's significant business processes during audit planning helps the auditor primarily to

answers.text: Prepare the entity's financial statements in accordance with the applicable reporting framework
Set the audit fee at a level that reflects the entity's operational complexity
Determine which management personnel should be disciplined for internal control deficiencies

Identify the classes of transactions, account balances, and disclosures that flow through each process, and the controls embedded in those processes that are relevant to the risk of material misstatement

explanations.a: Preparing financial statements is management's responsibility — not the auditor's. The auditor's understanding of business processes informs the risk assessment and the design of audit procedures, not the preparation of the statements.
explanations.b: Fee determination is a commercial matter influenced by engagement complexity and firm resources — it is not the primary purpose of understanding business processes from a professional standards perspective.
explanations.c: Recommending or determining personnel discipline is a management responsibility, not an audit function. The auditor may communicate control deficiencies to management and those charged with governance, but personnel decisions rest with management.
explanations.d: AU-C 315 requires the auditor to understand the entity's business processes that affect classes of transactions, account balances, and disclosures. This understanding enables the auditor to: identify which financial statement elements are affected by each process; identify the controls that management has designed to address process-specific risks; and design audit procedures that are responsive to the specific risks in each process. For example, understanding the revenue-to-cash collection process enables the auditor to identify controls over order acceptance, shipping, billing, and cash application — and to assess whether those controls adequately address the risks of misstatement in revenue and accounts receivable.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response
questions.keyword: business processes and internal control design
questions.text: An auditor performs walkthrough procedures for the entity's cash disbursements process. The PRIMARY purpose of these procedures is to

answers.text: Confirm the auditor's understanding of the process by tracing one or more transactions from initiation through recording — validating that documented process descriptions and controls actually reflect how the process operates in practice
Perform sufficient testing to allow the auditor to reduce substantive procedures for the cash disbursements cycle to zero
Satisfy the auditor's requirement to test 100% of all cash disbursements during the audit period
Generate evidence sufficient to conclude that no material misstatements exist in the accounts payable balance

explanations.a: A walkthrough (as defined in AU-C 315 and PCAOB AS 2201) involves tracing a transaction or a small number of transactions through the entire process from origination to recording in the financial statements. The purpose is to confirm the auditor's understanding of the process — specifically to validate that the documented process description and the controls identified in the risk assessment accurately reflect how the process actually functions. Walkthroughs are not designed to provide evidence sufficient to reach audit conclusions about account balances; they are understanding and design evaluation tools.
explanations.b: Walkthrough procedures confirm process understanding and evaluate control design — they are not tests of operating effectiveness. Even if the design appears sound, the auditor must also test operating effectiveness before reducing substantive procedures. A walkthrough alone cannot justify elimination of all substantive testing.
explanations.c: Walkthroughs typically involve tracing one or a small number of transactions — not 100% of transactions. The 100% coverage concept applies to certain substantive procedures in specific circumstances, not to walkthroughs, which are used to understand the process, not to test the completeness of processing.
explanations.d: Walkthroughs inform the auditor about process design — they do not directly provide audit evidence about account balances. Evidence about the accounts payable balance is obtained through substantive procedures (such as agreeing selected amounts to vendor invoices, performing accounts payable confirmations, or reviewing subsequent payments).

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response
questions.keyword: business processes and internal control design
questions.text: A small entity assigns one employee the responsibility for both authorizing purchase orders and approving vendor invoices for payment. From an internal control design perspective, this arrangement represents

answers.text: An acceptable compensating control because the employee's dual roles provide end-to-end visibility over the procurement process

A segregation of duties weakness — combining authorization and payment approval functions creates the opportunity for that individual to initiate and approve fraudulent disbursements without independent detection
An effective control because small entities are exempt from segregation of duties requirements under GAAS
An authorization control that enhances the reliability of the accounts payable balance by ensuring consistency between purchase orders and approved invoices

explanations.a: Having end-to-end visibility is not the same as a compensating control. A compensating control addresses a segregation of duties weakness through a different mechanism — for example, management review of all disbursements above a threshold by an independent party. The dual role itself is not a compensating control; it is the deficiency that requires compensation.
explanations.b: Segregation of duties is one of the most important preventive controls in any disbursements process. The purpose of separating the authorization of purchase orders from the approval of vendor invoices is to ensure that two independent judgments are applied — one to the commitment of resources (the purchase) and one to the obligation to pay (the invoice). When one person performs both functions, that individual can authorize a fictitious or fraudulent purchase and subsequently approve payment for it without any independent review, creating an undetected opportunity for misappropriation.
explanations.c: Small entities are not exempt from segregation of duties requirements. However, GAAS acknowledges that small entities may have inherent limitations in implementing full segregation of duties due to limited staff — and in such cases, compensating controls (such as active owner oversight of all disbursements) should be implemented. The absence of segregation is still a control deficiency that must be documented and communicated.
explanations.d: An individual approving both purchase orders and vendor invoices does not enhance reliability — it removes the independent check that would detect unauthorized or fictitious transactions. Consistency between purchase orders and invoices approved by the same person does not indicate that either the purchase or the invoice is legitimate.

questions.text: An auditor evaluates the payroll process and determines that the design of controls — segregation of duties, authorization requirements, and reconciliation procedures — appears adequate to prevent and detect material misstatements. Testing of a sample of payroll transactions then reveals that three key reconciliation procedures were not performed consistently during the year. What conclusion should the auditor draw?

answers.text: The controls can still be relied upon because the design is sound — operating failures in three instances are not sufficient to undermine overall control reliance
The auditor should increase the payroll testing sample size until no additional exceptions are found, at which point controls can be relied upon

Controls that are well-designed but not operating effectively do not provide reliable protection — the auditor should evaluate the severity of the operating failures, assess whether a significant deficiency or material weakness exists, and expand substantive payroll testing
The design adequacy assessment is the more important conclusion — operating failures in reconciliation are always immaterial because reconciliations are detective rather than preventive controls

explanations.a: Sound control design is necessary but not sufficient for auditor reliance. A control that is well-designed but not consistently operated provides no assurance about the periods when it was not performed. The auditor must evaluate both design and operating effectiveness — AU-C 330 requires tests of operating effectiveness before concluding that a control can be relied upon to reduce substantive procedures.
explanations.b: Increasing the sample until no additional exceptions are found is not a valid methodology. Each exception found in a sample has implications for the entire population. The appropriate response to control exceptions is to understand their nature and implications, assess whether they indicate a systemic failure, and determine whether to modify the substantive testing approach accordingly.
explanations.c: Controls can only reduce substantive testing if they are both designed effectively AND operating effectively throughout the period. Operating failures — even in a sample — indicate that the controls cannot be relied upon for the periods and transactions where they failed. The auditor must: evaluate whether the failures are indicative of a significant deficiency or material weakness; determine whether the failures were isolated or systematic; and expand substantive payroll testing to obtain sufficient evidence for the payroll-related assertions without reliance on the failed controls.
explanations.d: Reconciliation controls are important detective controls — they identify mismatements after they have occurred so they can be corrected. When reconciliation controls fail to operate, errors or irregularities that occurred during the period may not have been detected and corrected. The failure of detective controls increases the risk that misstatements exist in the financial statements, which is not immaterial regardless of whether the controls are preventive or detective.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response
questions.keyword: business processes and internal control design
questions.text: An entity relies on an automated three-way match control in its accounts payable system — which compares the purchase order, receiving report, and vendor invoice before allowing payment. ITGCs are assessed as effective. If this automated control is tested and found to be operating effectively throughout the year, the auditor should

answers.text: Eliminate all substantive testing of accounts payable since effective automated controls provide absolute assurance over disbursements
Expand substantive testing of accounts payable to confirm that the automated control is actually working
Increase the audit fee to reflect the additional value created by the effective automated control

Consider whether the effective automated control and strong ITGCs support reducing the scope of substantive accounts payable testing — while recognizing that some level of substantive testing is still required regardless of control reliance

explanations.a: Effective automated controls reduce but do not eliminate the need for substantive testing. AU-C 330 requires the auditor to design and perform substantive procedures for all significant accounts regardless of assessed control risk — the nature, timing, and extent of those procedures may be reduced when controls are effective, but substantive procedures cannot be entirely eliminated.
explanations.b: If the auditor has tested the automated control and found it effective (and ITGCs support that the control operated consistently throughout the period), expanding substantive testing would be inconsistent with the audit evidence obtained. The appropriate response to effective controls is to reduce substantive testing, not expand it.
explanations.c: Audit fee determination is a commercial matter based on engagement effort, risk, and resources — not a professional standards response to effective controls.
explanations.d: This is the correct application of the audit risk model under AU-C 330. When automated controls are effective and supported by effective ITGCs, the auditor obtains persuasive evidence that the accounts payable process — for the transactions within the scope of the automated control — is functioning as designed. This supports reducing the nature, timing, and extent of substantive procedures (for example, reducing sample sizes for detailed testing, performing analytical procedures rather than detailed tests for lower-risk disbursements, or confirming fewer accounts payable balances). However, the auditor must still perform some substantive procedures — AU-C 330.18 specifically requires substantive procedures for all significant account balances, classes of transactions, and disclosures regardless of the assessment of control risk.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response
questions.text: In the context of AU-C Section 402, a service organization is BEST described as

answers.text: A third-party entity that provides services that are part of the user entity's information system relevant to financial reporting — such as a payroll processor, cloud data center, loan servicer, or transfer agent
Any external vendor that supplies goods or services to the audit client, regardless of whether those services affect financial reporting
A governmental entity that regulates and monitors the user entity's industry
The audit firm engaged to perform the audit of the service organization's own financial statements

explanations.a: AU-C Section 402 defines a service organization as a third-party organization or segment of an organization that provides services to user entities that are likely to be relevant to those entities' internal control over financial reporting. Relevant services include processing transactions (payroll processors, investment custodians, loan servicers), maintaining records (transfer agents, data centers), or executing and recording transactions on behalf of the user entity. The key criterion is that the service affects the user entity's financial reporting.
explanations.b: Not every external vendor is a service organization under AU-C 402. A supplier of raw materials or office supplies does not affect the user entity's information system or financial reporting in a way that is relevant to AU-C 402 — the standard applies specifically to services that are part of the user entity's information system relevant to financial reporting.
explanations.c: A regulatory body that monitors the industry is not a service organization under AU-C 402. Regulatory entities exercise authority over the user entity but do not process transactions on its behalf or form part of its information system.
explanations.d: The audit firm performing the audit of the service organization's own financial statements is the service auditor — not the service organization itself. The service organization is the entity providing services to user entities.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response
questions.text: A SOC 1 Type 1 report differs from a SOC 1 Type 2 report primarily in that

answers.text: A Type 1 report is issued by the user entity's auditor; a Type 2 is issued by an independent service auditor
A Type 1 covers a single significant account; a Type 2 covers all accounts in the financial statements

A Type 1 report addresses control design and the fairness of the description as of a specified date; a Type 2 additionally covers the operating effectiveness of controls over a period — making a Type 2 necessary for the user auditor to rely on service organization controls
A Type 1 report is publicly available; a Type 2 report is restricted to the user entity's management only

explanations.a: Both Type 1 and Type 2 SOC 1 reports are issued by an independent service auditor — not by the user entity's auditor. The user auditor uses the service auditor's report as audit evidence.
explanations.b: The distinction between Type 1 and Type 2 is not based on coverage of specific accounts. Both types address the service organization's controls over the user entities' financial reporting in general, not individual accounts.
explanations.c: A SOC 1 Type 1 report (SSAE 18 AT-C Section 320) provides the service auditor's opinion on: (1) whether the description of the service organization's system fairly presents the system as designed and implemented; and (2) whether the controls described are suitably designed to achieve their control objectives — evaluated as of a specific date. A Type 2 report provides everything in a Type 1 plus an opinion on whether those controls operated effectively throughout a specified period. The user auditor needs a Type 2 to obtain audit evidence about whether service organization controls were operating effectively during the audit period.
explanations.d: SOC 1 reports (both Type 1 and Type 2) are restricted-use reports available to management of the user entity and their auditors — they are not publicly available. This is different from SOC 3 reports, which are general-use public-availability reports.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response
questions.text: A user auditor receives a SOC 1 Type 2 report covering controls at a payroll service organization. Before reducing tests of controls over payroll, the user auditor must ALSO consider

answers.text: Whether complementary user entity controls (CUECs) identified in the report are implemented and operating effectively at the user entity — because the service organization's controls may not achieve their objectives without those CUECs
Whether the service auditor's report should be re-performed by the user auditor to confirm accuracy
Whether to request that the service organization become a subsidiary of the user entity to simplify reporting
Whether the service auditor's opinion letter meets the user auditor's preferred formatting standards

explanations.a: SOC 1 reports frequently identify complementary user entity controls (CUECs) — controls that the user entity must have in place for the service organization's controls to achieve their stated objectives. For example, a payroll processor's controls may only be effective if the user entity maintains controls over the authorization of new hires and salary changes before they are transmitted to the processor. The user auditor must test these CUECs at the user entity level — they are not addressed in the service auditor's report and are the user entity's responsibility.
explanations.b: The user auditor does not re-perform the service auditor's work — the service auditor's report is used as audit evidence. The user auditor may evaluate the competence and independence of the service auditor but does not independently recreate the service audit.
explanations.c: A service organization's corporate relationship with the user entity has no bearing on the audit evidence needed. Changing the organizational relationship would not affect the audit procedure requirements under AU-C 402.
explanations.d: Formatting standards are administrative preferences with no bearing on the auditor's substantive evaluation of whether service organization controls can be relied upon to reduce tests of controls at the user entity.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response
questions.text: A user entity processes all of its investment transactions through a significant custodian and transfer agent. The user auditor requests a SOC 1 Type 2 report but learns none is available. Which course of action is MOST appropriate?

answers.text: Accept management's representation that the service organization's controls are effective and issue an unmodified opinion
Immediately issue a qualified opinion because the absence of a SOC 1 report is itself a material misstatement
Perform all audit procedures at the user entity level only, ignoring the service organization entirely

Visit the service organization to directly test its relevant controls, arrange for another auditor to test them, or significantly expand substantive testing of the affected accounts — and if sufficient evidence cannot be obtained, consider the effect on the opinion

explanations.a: Management's representation is not sufficient evidence for the operating effectiveness of service organization controls. The user auditor must obtain independent evidence — either through a SOC 1 report, direct testing, or other means. Relying solely on management's assertion would not constitute sufficient appropriate audit evidence.
explanations.b: The absence of a SOC 1 report is not itself a material misstatement — it is an audit evidence gap. The appropriate response is to find alternative means of obtaining the needed evidence. An opinion modification would only be appropriate if the user auditor cannot obtain sufficient evidence by any means.
explanations.c: Ignoring the service organization is not an option when it processes transactions significant to the financial statements. AU-C 402 requires the user auditor to obtain an understanding of the service organization's controls relevant to the user entity's financial reporting.
explanations.d: AU-C Section 402 specifies that when a SOC 1 report is unavailable for a significant service organization, the user auditor may: (1) visit the service organization and directly test the relevant controls; (2) use another auditor to perform procedures at the service organization; or (3) perform additional substantive procedures at the user entity to obtain sufficient evidence about the affected accounts without relying on service organization controls. If none of these alternatives can provide sufficient evidence, the auditor considers the effect on the audit opinion, potentially leading to a qualified opinion or disclaimer.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response
questions.text: A user entity's fiscal year ends December 31. The SOC 1 Type 2 report from the payroll service organization covers April 1 through September 30 — leaving a three-month gap to year-end. How should the user auditor address this gap?

answers.text: Accept the SOC 1 report as covering the full audit period since it covers more than half the year
Disregard the SOC 1 report entirely and perform direct tests of the service organization's controls for the full year

Request a bridge letter from the service auditor covering October 1 through December 31, inquire about significant changes at the service organization during the gap period, and consider whether additional procedures are needed if the bridge letter indicates changes
Restrict the audit opinion to cover only the period addressed by the SOC 1 report (April 1 through September 30)

explanations.a: A SOC 1 report that does not cover the full audit period cannot be used as evidence for the uncovered period. The user auditor must obtain additional evidence for the October 1 through December 31 gap.
explanations.b: Performing direct tests of service organization controls for the full year is one option but is more invasive and costly than first pursuing a bridge letter. The bridge letter approach is the standard professional response to a period gap in a SOC 1 report.
explanations.c: When a SOC 1 Type 2 report does not cover the full audit period, the user auditor should: (1) request a bridge letter from the service auditor for the gap period — the bridge letter provides the service auditor's representations about whether any changes to the service organization's system or controls occurred during the gap period that would affect the conclusions in the SOC 1 report; (2) inquire of management about significant changes at the service organization; and (3) if the bridge letter or other information indicates significant changes, perform additional procedures to address those changes. If no significant changes occurred, the user auditor may be able to extend reliance on the SOC 1 report to the gap period.
explanations.d: Restricting the audit opinion to the period covered by the SOC 1 report is not a standard option — the audit opinion covers the full fiscal year. The user auditor must find a way to address the gap period, not limit the scope of the opinion.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response
questions.text: A user entity outsources its IT infrastructure to a cloud provider. The SOC 1 Type 2 report for the cloud provider identifies three complementary user entity controls (CUECs): (1) the user entity must manage its own user access provisioning; (2) the user entity must monitor system logs for unusual activity; and (3) the user entity must perform data backups for data not covered by the provider. The user auditor confirms that the user entity has not implemented any of these three CUECs. Which assessment is MOST appropriate?

answers.text: The absence of the CUECs is inconsequential because the cloud provider's Type 2 report already confirms that controls are operating effectively

The cloud provider's controls may not be achieving their stated control objectives without the CUECs — the user auditor cannot rely on the provider's controls for the assertions affected by these gaps and must significantly expand substantive procedures to compensate
The user auditor should report the absent CUECs to the cloud provider and request the provider implement the CUECs on behalf of the user entity
The user entity is exempt from CUEC requirements if it is a small entity with fewer than 50 employees

explanations.a: This misunderstands the relationship between service organization controls and CUECs. A SOC 1 Type 2 report confirms that the service organization's controls are designed and operating effectively — but those controls are designed to work in conjunction with the CUECs. The report explicitly states that its conclusions depend on the user entity implementing the identified CUECs. Without them, the service organization's controls alone may be insufficient to achieve the stated control objectives.
explanations.b: CUECs are controls that the user entity must have in place for the service organization's controls to function as intended. Without user access provisioning controls (CUEC 1), unauthorized users may access the cloud systems even if the provider's infrastructure is secure. Without log monitoring (CUEC 2), unauthorized activity would go undetected. Without data backup controls (CUEC 3), data integrity cannot be assured for uncovered data. The absence of all three CUECs means the user entity cannot rely on the cloud provider's controls for the assertions those CUECs support. The user auditor must: document the absent CUECs as control deficiencies; communicate them to management and TCWG; and significantly expand substantive testing of the affected accounts and transactions.
explanations.c: CUECs are the user entity's responsibility — not the service organization's. The service auditor identifies them as controls that user entities are expected to implement. It is not the cloud provider's role to implement controls that belong to the user entity's governance structure.
explanations.d: CUEC requirements apply to all user entities regardless of size. There is no small-entity exemption from the need to implement CUECs identified in a SOC 1 report for controls the auditor seeks to rely upon.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response
questions.keyword: limitations of controls and management override risk
questions.text: Which of the following is an inherent limitation of internal control that prevents it from providing absolute assurance, regardless of how well controls are designed?

answers.text: The absence of a written accounting policy manual
Failure to engage an external audit firm
Insufficient number of employees in the accounting department
The possibility of human error, collusion among employees to circumvent controls, or management override of controls

explanations.a: The absence of written policies is a control deficiency, not an inherent limitation of internal control. Written policies can be implemented — their absence reflects a design choice, not an unavoidable constraint.
explanations.b: The external audit is a monitoring mechanism — not an internal control, and its absence is not an inherent limitation of the internal control system. External audits supplement but are separate from internal controls.
explanations.c: Insufficient staffing is a practical constraint that may result in inadequate segregation of duties — it is a condition that can potentially be addressed through compensating controls or additional hiring, not an inherent limitation applicable to all entities.
explanations.d: The COSO framework and auditing standards recognize three categories of inherent limitations that prevent internal control from providing absolute assurance regardless of design quality: (1) human error — even well-intentioned individuals make mistakes in judgment and performance; (2) collusion — multiple individuals working together can circumvent controls that rely on one person checking another; and (3) management override — management has the authority to override the very controls it established. These limitations cannot be designed away, which is why audits supplement but do not rely exclusively on internal control.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response
questions.keyword: limitations of controls and management override risk
questions.text: Management override risk is treated as uniquely significant in audit planning because

answers.text: Management has the authority and ability to bypass controls they themselves designed and implemented — including automated controls — and this risk cannot be eliminated through control design alone, requiring specific override-responsive audit procedures in every audit
Management override only occurs in entities with weak governance structures and can be addressed by confirming that an active audit committee is in place
Management override is limited to manual journal entries and does not affect automated transaction processing systems
Management override risk is only relevant in industries with a history of financial statement fraud

explanations.a: AU-C Section 240 specifically identifies management override as a significant fraud risk in every audit because of its unique characteristics: management designed the control system and therefore knows its gaps; management has the authority to authorize exceptions; and management can instruct employees to bypass controls. Because management sits above the control environment, even the most sophisticated control systems cannot prevent management override — this is an inherent limitation. AU-C 240 therefore requires specific procedures to address this risk (journal entry testing, estimate review for bias, and retrospective review of estimates) regardless of the assessed control environment.
explanations.b: Active audit committees and strong governance reduce the risk that management override will occur or go undetected — but they do not eliminate the risk. Even entities with effective audit committees face management override risk because the audit committee does not monitor every transaction. The risk is universal, not limited to weak governance structures.
explanations.c: Management override can affect automated systems as well as manual processes. Management can override automated controls by: directing IT staff to make unauthorized program changes; creating manual journal entries that bypass automated controls; or using system administrator access to process transactions outside normal workflows.
explanations.d: Management override risk is a required fraud risk consideration in every audit regardless of industry. AU-C 240 requires the auditor to presume that risks of fraud in revenue recognition and from management override exist in all audits — it is not an industry-specific concern.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response
questions.keyword: limitations of controls and management override risk
questions.text: Under AU-C Section 240, which procedures must the auditor perform in EVERY audit regardless of the assessed level of fraud risk?

answers.text: Performing forensic accounting procedures and interviewing all accounting personnel
Engaging a fraud investigation specialist before beginning field work

Testing journal entries and other adjustments for appropriateness, reviewing accounting estimates for management bias, and evaluating the business rationale for significant unusual transactions — particularly near period-end
Obtaining written representations from all members of the board of directors regarding their personal knowledge of fraud

explanations.a: Forensic accounting procedures and comprehensive employee interviews are investigative responses to identified fraud — they are not required in every audit regardless of fraud risk level. These intensive measures are applied when specific fraud risk factors are identified or when fraud is suspected.
explanations.b: Engaging a fraud specialist before field work is not a universal requirement. A specialist may be used when specific fraud risks warrant specialized expertise, but it is not mandated in every audit.
explanations.c: AU-C Section 240.28-.32 specifies procedures required in every audit as responses to the inherent risk of management override: (1) test journal entries and other adjustments, focusing on unusual entries, those recorded by personnel without authority, and entries made near period-end — to detect unauthorized adjustments; (2) review accounting estimates for management bias — by retrospectively reviewing prior-period estimates and considering whether current-period estimates reflect a consistent pattern; and (3) for significant transactions outside the normal course of business, evaluate whether the business rationale is genuine or whether the transaction may be structured to achieve financial reporting objectives.
explanations.d: Written representations from board members about personal knowledge of fraud are not a required procedure in every audit. The auditor obtains written representations from management and, where appropriate, those charged with governance under AU-C 580 — but not personal fraud attestations from all board members.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response
questions.keyword: limitations of controls and management override risk
questions.text: An auditor assesses that a company has a strong control environment, an active and independent audit committee, and effective monitoring activities. How does this positive assessment affect the auditor's approach to management override risk?

answers.text: A strong control environment reduces management override risk to an acceptable level — specific override-responsive procedures are not required when governance is strong
The positive assessment allows the auditor to rely entirely on internal controls and eliminate all substantive procedures
The auditor may reduce the extent of fraud risk assessment procedures since the strong governance structure provides inherent protection against override

Management override risk remains a required consideration regardless of control environment quality — the inherent nature of override means it cannot be controlled away, and AU-C 240 override-specific procedures remain required even in the strongest control environments

explanations.a: This incorrectly describes the treatment of management override risk. AU-C 240 explicitly states that management override is presumed to be a significant risk in all audits and that specific procedures to address this risk are required regardless of assessed control environment quality. A strong control environment reduces the likelihood of override occurring undetected, but does not eliminate the inherent risk that management could override controls if motivated to do so.
explanations.b: Eliminating all substantive procedures based solely on control assessment is not permitted. AU-C 330 requires substantive procedures for all significant accounts regardless of assessed control risk. Additionally, the management override inherent limitation means substantive procedures serve the critical function of detecting misstatements that might exist despite effective controls.
explanations.c: AU-C 240 does not provide for reducing fraud risk assessment procedures based on governance quality alone. While governance is a relevant fraud risk factor, the brainstorming session and fraud risk assessment procedures are required in every audit.
explanations.d: The COSO framework and AU-C 240 acknowledge that management override is an inherent limitation of internal control — meaning it cannot be eliminated through control design, regardless of how strong the overall system is. Since management sits above the controls, a determined management team can always find a way to bypass controls they have authority over. AU-C 240 therefore requires override-specific procedures (journal entry testing, estimate bias review, unusual transaction review) in every audit without exception.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response
questions.keyword: limitations of controls and management override risk
questions.text: An auditor notes that management routinely makes unsupported journal entries to revenue accounts near year-end, with explanations such as 'accruals' or 'corrections' but no underlying documentation. How should the auditor respond to this pattern?

answers.text: Accept the entries as management's prerogative since management is responsible for the financial statements and has authority over journal entries
Request that management provide written representations confirming that all journal entries are appropriate
Document the pattern but defer additional procedures to the following year when more information will be available

Expand journal entry testing with a focus on entries affecting revenue, apply heightened professional skepticism, obtain documentation or explanations for the unsupported entries, and consider whether the pattern indicates intentional revenue manipulation requiring more extensive fraud-responsive procedures

explanations.a: Management's authority over journal entries does not mean the auditor must accept them without scrutiny. Journal entries — particularly unsupported ones affecting revenue near period-end — are a primary mechanism of financial statement fraud. The auditor's responsibility to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence includes independently evaluating the propriety of significant journal entries.
explanations.b: Written representations from management are insufficient to resolve concerns about potentially fraudulent journal entries. If management has already made unsupported adjustments, their written representations on those same adjustments provide no independent corroboration. The auditor needs independent evidence — supporting documentation and business rationale — not management attestations.
explanations.c: Deferring procedures to a future year leaves the current-year financial statements potentially misstated. AU-C 240 requires the auditor to address identified fraud risk indicators in the current engagement — not to carry them forward.
explanations.d: Unsupported journal entries to revenue accounts near year-end are one of the strongest fraud risk indicators identified in AU-C 240. The appropriate response includes: expanding the scope of journal entry testing to cover all entries affecting revenue, particularly period-end entries; requesting supporting documentation for each identified unsupported entry; evaluating the business rationale for each entry; looking for patterns (recurring unsupported entries, entries that inflate results close to targets); and considering whether the pattern — combined with other fraud risk factors — indicates that revenue is being intentionally manipulated, which would require more extensive procedures and discussion with the engagement partner.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response
questions.keyword: materiality for financial statements as a whole
questions.text: For financial reporting purposes, information is considered material if

answers.text: It represents a line item that appears on the face of the income statement or balance sheet
Its omission, misstatement, or non-disclosure could reasonably be expected to influence the economic decisions of users made on the basis of the financial statements
It exceeds 10% of the entity's total assets, which is the universal materiality threshold established by the FASB
It is disclosed in the notes to the financial statements rather than on the face of the primary statements

explanations.a: The location of information on the face of the financial statements versus a note does not determine materiality. Information in notes can be material (and omission of required disclosures is a form of material misstatement), while certain line items on the face may not be material.
explanations.b: AU-C Section 320 adopts the conceptual definition of materiality: information is material if its omission or misstatement could reasonably be expected to influence the economic decisions of financial statement users. This definition requires consideration of both the magnitude of the misstatement and the specific circumstances of the entity and its users — not just an arithmetic calculation.
explanations.c: There is no universal 10% threshold established by the FASB or any standard-setter. Materiality is an entity-specific, judgment-based determination that varies by entity, financial statement user, and the nature of the misstatement. While rules of thumb are sometimes used as starting points, no single universal threshold applies to all entities.
explanations.d: Whether information is disclosed in the notes rather than the primary statements does not determine materiality. Disclosures in notes can be material, and misstatements on the face of the statements can be immaterial — the criterion is the potential effect on user decisions, not the location of the information.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response
questions.keyword: materiality for financial statements as a whole
questions.text: When determining a quantitative materiality threshold, the auditor selects a benchmark and applies a percentage to that benchmark. Common benchmarks used include

answers.text: Pre-tax income from continuing operations, total revenues, total assets, and equity — selected based on which benchmark best reflects the users' primary focus given the entity's nature and circumstances
The auditor's billable hours on the engagement and the entity's market capitalization
The number of employees and total payroll expense
The external auditor's assessment of management's competence and the entity's credit rating

explanations.a: AU-C Section 320 indicates that the auditor identifies a benchmark appropriate to the entity's circumstances. Common benchmarks include: pre-tax income from continuing operations (appropriate when users focus on profitability); total revenues or gross profit (useful when income is volatile or when revenue is the primary indicator of size and performance); total assets (appropriate for balance-sheet-oriented entities such as financial institutions); equity or net assets (relevant for some entities where net asset value is the primary focus); and payroll expense (for nonprofit entities). The appropriate benchmark reflects what financial statement users care most about.
explanations.b: The auditor's billable hours and the entity's market capitalization are not recognized benchmarks for materiality determination. Market capitalization is sometimes used as a supplemental consideration for publicly traded companies but is not a standard standalone materiality benchmark.
explanations.c: Number of employees and total payroll are not primary materiality benchmarks. While payroll expense may be used in specific contexts (e.g., for labor-intensive nonprofits), headcount is not a standard financial benchmark for materiality.
explanations.d: The auditor's assessment of management's competence and the entity's credit rating are audit risk factors and business context considerations — they are not quantitative benchmarks for materiality determination.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response
questions.keyword: materiality for financial statements as a whole
questions.text: An entity operates in the hotel industry and experiences highly volatile earnings — income ranges from a $10 million profit to a $5 million loss depending on the year. The auditor is determining the appropriate materiality benchmark. Which benchmark is MOST appropriate in this situation?

answers.text: Pre-tax income — because it directly reflects the entity's financial performance
Total payroll expense — because labor is the largest cost in the hotel industry
Number of hotel rooms — because capacity is the most meaningful metric for industry analysts

Total revenues — because the volatility of earnings makes pre-tax income an unreliable benchmark, and revenue more consistently reflects the entity's size and the users' primary interest in understanding financial performance

explanations.a: When earnings are highly volatile — ranging from significant profits to significant losses depending on the year — applying a fixed percentage to pre-tax income produces extremely inconsistent materiality amounts. A low or negative income year would produce a very low materiality amount, potentially leading to over-auditing; a high-income year would produce a high materiality amount. This inconsistency makes pre-tax income an unreliable benchmark for entities with volatile earnings.
explanations.b: Total payroll expense may be used in specific contexts where payroll is the primary focus — such as for a labor union or certain government entities. For a hotel company where users focus on total operating performance, revenue is a more appropriate primary benchmark.
explanations.c: Number of hotel rooms (or any non-financial operating metric) is not a standard financial materiality benchmark. Materiality benchmarks are financial statement amounts, not physical operational metrics.
explanations.d: When an entity has highly volatile earnings, total revenues provide a more stable and consistent benchmark because they do not fluctuate as dramatically as net income. For a hotel company, revenues consistently reflect the scale of operations and are a primary indicator that financial statement users examine to understand performance. Using revenues produces a more consistent materiality level across periods, allowing for more comparable audit coverage year over year.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response
questions.keyword: materiality for financial statements as a whole
questions.text: A misstatement may be considered material even when the dollar amount is below the quantitative materiality threshold. This is BEST explained by which concept?

answers.text: There are no circumstances in which a misstatement below the quantitative threshold can be considered material
Auditors may lower their materiality threshold at any time based on their professional preferences

Qualitative factors may make a numerically small misstatement material — for example, if the misstatement converts a reported profit to a loss, causes the entity to breach a debt covenant, involves transactions with related parties, or affects management's compliance with regulatory requirements
All misstatements must be corrected regardless of dollar amount, making quantitative thresholds irrelevant

explanations.a: The quantitative threshold is a guide, not an absolute rule. Professional standards explicitly acknowledge that qualitative factors can make a numerically small misstatement material. An absolute rule that everything below the threshold is immaterial would ignore circumstances where the nature of the misstatement — rather than its size — would influence user decisions.
explanations.b: Materiality thresholds are determined based on professional judgment and objective criteria — not personal preferences. Arbitrary lowering of materiality without basis would undermine the consistency and reliability of the audit.
explanations.c: Qualitative materiality is a well-established concept in AU-C 320 and SEC Staff Accounting Bulletin 99. Even a dollar amount below the quantitative threshold may be material based on qualitative factors: (1) a misstatement that causes a reported loss to become a reported profit (or vice versa) is likely material because it changes the directional signal of performance; (2) a misstatement that causes the entity to violate a debt covenant is material because of the potential legal and financial consequences; (3) related-party transactions are qualitatively significant regardless of amount because they involve conflicts of interest that users need to assess; (4) misstatements that affect management's compliance with regulatory requirements are material because of their legal and reputational implications.
explanations.d: Professional standards do not require correcting all misstatements regardless of amount. Rather, misstatements that are quantitatively and qualitatively immaterial need not be corrected, though management typically corrects them as a quality matter. Requiring correction of all errors regardless of amount would be impractical and is not the standard.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response
questions.keyword: materiality for financial statements as a whole
questions.text: An auditor establishes preliminary overall materiality at $500,000 based on estimated pre-tax income of $5 million (10% benchmark application). During the audit, the auditor learns that actual pre-tax income is $1.5 million — significantly below the estimate used to set materiality. How should the auditor respond?

answers.text: Continue using the original $500,000 materiality since it was established in good faith based on available information at the time

Revise overall materiality to approximately $150,000 (10% of actual $1.5 million income), assess whether additional audit procedures are needed to address the revised level, and consider communicating the change to those charged with governance
Issue a qualified opinion because the change in actual income indicates management manipulated earnings to meet the materiality threshold
Automatically expand all tests to 100% of transactions to compensate for the reduced income

explanations.a: Using the original materiality when actual results are significantly different from the estimate would result in an audit that does not adequately address the actual financial results. If actual income is $1.5 million instead of the estimated $5 million, a $500,000 misstatement represents 33% of actual income — far above what would be material relative to the actual reported results. Continuing with the original threshold would risk missing material misstatements.
explanations.b: AU-C Section 320 requires the auditor to revise materiality during the audit if information obtained makes the original determination inappropriate. When actual results differ significantly from the estimate, the auditor should: recalculate materiality using actual results ($1.5M × 10% = $150,000); assess whether the lower materiality affects planned procedures (e.g., whether prior tests were designed to detect misstatements at the new threshold); determine whether additional procedures are needed for accounts where the original testing may have been insufficient; and communicate the change to those charged with governance if appropriate.
explanations.c: A difference between estimated and actual income does not indicate earnings manipulation — businesses regularly have actual results that differ from forecasts. An opinion modification would be issued only if the auditor identifies evidence of actual misstatement, not merely because results differed from the planning estimate.
explanations.d: Expanding all tests to 100% of transactions is not the proportionate or required response. The auditor revises materiality and then reassesses which procedures need to be expanded based on risk and the new threshold — not blanket 100% coverage across all areas.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response
questions.text: Performance materiality differs from overall materiality in that performance materiality

answers.text: Is always set at exactly 50% of overall materiality per AICPA rules
Applies only to disclosures in the notes to the financial statements
Is set at the same amount as overall materiality for efficiency purposes

Is set below overall materiality to reduce the risk that the aggregate of uncorrected and undetected misstatements exceeds overall materiality — reflecting the auditor's recognition that misstatements may occur in multiple areas simultaneously

explanations.a: Performance materiality is not set at any fixed percentage mandated by professional standards. AU-C 320 requires it to be less than overall materiality and established based on the auditor's judgment — common practice may result in amounts around 50-75% of overall materiality, but no specific percentage is prescribed.
explanations.b: Performance materiality applies to the audit procedures for all areas of the financial statements — not just disclosures. It is the threshold used to design the nature and extent of procedures across all accounts and assertions.
explanations.c: Setting performance materiality at the same level as overall materiality would defeat its purpose. If the auditor tests each area to the overall materiality threshold, the aggregate of misstatements in multiple areas could exceed overall materiality — performance materiality creates a buffer to prevent this outcome.
explanations.d: AU-C Section 320 defines performance materiality as the amount or amounts set below overall materiality to reduce the probability that the aggregate of uncorrected and undetected misstatements in the financial statements exceeds overall materiality. The rationale is that misstatements are unlikely to be found in only one account — they may exist simultaneously in multiple areas. If each area is tested to the overall materiality level, the aggregate of misstatements found across all areas could exceed overall materiality. Performance materiality creates a margin of safety by testing each area to a lower threshold.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response
questions.text: An auditor sets overall materiality at $400,000 and performance materiality at $280,000 (70% of overall). The auditor is designing sample sizes for testing accounts receivable. Tolerable misstatement for this specific procedure is set at $250,000. Which statement BEST describes the relationship between these three amounts?

answers.text: The three amounts are independent — tolerable misstatement may be higher than overall materiality for specific high-risk areas
Tolerable misstatement for a specific procedure is derived from performance materiality and is always equal to overall materiality divided by two

Tolerable misstatement ($250,000) is the application of performance materiality to the specific accounts receivable procedure — it is set at or below performance materiality ($280,000), and both are below overall materiality ($400,000), creating a layered safety buffer for the aggregate of misstatements
The sample size is determined solely by the dollar value of accounts receivable — the materiality amounts are used only for reporting purposes

explanations.a: Tolerable misstatement for any specific procedure cannot exceed overall materiality. These amounts are hierarchically related: overall materiality sets the upper bound, performance materiality is set below it, and tolerable misstatement for specific procedures is set at or below performance materiality.
explanations.b: Tolerable misstatement is not calculated using a fixed formula relative to overall materiality. It is a judgment-based application of performance materiality to a specific procedure, considering the risk of misstatement in the account and the expected frequency and amount of misstatements.
explanations.c: This accurately describes the hierarchical relationship. Overall materiality ($400,000) is the highest level — a misstatement at or above this amount in the financial statements as a whole would be considered material. Performance materiality ($280,000) is set below overall materiality to create a buffer for the aggregate of misstatements across all areas. Tolerable misstatement for accounts receivable ($250,000) is the application of performance materiality to the specific accounts receivable testing procedure — it is the maximum amount of misstatement the auditor is willing to accept in that account before concluding that the balance is materially misstated.
explanations.d: Sample sizes in monetary unit sampling (and other sampling methods) are directly influenced by tolerable misstatement — a lower tolerable misstatement requires a larger sample to provide the same level of assurance. The materiality amounts are not only for reporting purposes; they are fundamental inputs to sampling design.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response
questions.text: An auditor is planning tests of accounts payable and sets tolerable misstatement at $150,000. After performing testing, the auditor finds projected misstatements of $130,000 — which is below tolerable misstatement. However, the auditor also notes that the nature of the misstatements (understatement of accounts payable) is systematic, appearing in a large proportion of sampled items. How should the auditor evaluate this result?

answers.text: Since the projected misstatement ($130,000) is below tolerable misstatement ($150,000), the testing is complete and no further procedures are needed

The systematic nature of the misstatements — which affects a large proportion of sampled items — indicates that the projected misstatement may understate the true population error; the auditor should consider whether the testing results are reliable and whether additional procedures are needed to more accurately project the population error
The auditor should automatically qualify the opinion because any systematic misstatement indicates fraudulent financial reporting
The auditor should increase tolerable misstatement to $165,000 to accommodate the projected misstatement without additional work

explanations.a: A projected misstatement below tolerable misstatement does not automatically conclude testing. The nature of misstatements — particularly a systematic pattern affecting many items — is as important as the projected amount. A systematic misstatement indicates that the error affects the entire population, not just a random subset — and may suggest the statistical projection is unreliable or that the issue is more pervasive than the projection suggests.
explanations.b: When misstatements exhibit a systematic pattern — appearing consistently across a large proportion of sampled items — the auditor must consider several things: (1) the projection method assumes that sampled misstatements are representative of the population; a systematic pattern across many items may indicate the projected misstatement understates the actual population error; (2) a systematic understatement of accounts payable could indicate either a control failure or an intentional attempt to understate liabilities; (3) the auditor should consider whether the sample was representative, whether the projection is reliable, and whether the systematic pattern has implications for fraud risk — potentially warranting expansion of testing or a change in the population being tested.
explanations.c: A systematic misstatement does not automatically indicate fraud. It may reflect a systematic processing error, a misunderstanding of an accounting requirement, or inadequate controls — not necessarily intentional manipulation. The auditor must investigate the cause before drawing conclusions about fraud.
explanations.d: Increasing tolerable misstatement to accommodate projected misstatements without additional work is contrary to the purpose of the materiality framework. Tolerable misstatement is set based on performance materiality and risk assessment — not adjusted upward to allow projected misstatements to appear acceptable.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response
questions.text: An auditor is testing inventory and sets tolerable misstatement at $200,000. The test reveals an overstatement of $185,000 — below tolerable misstatement. The inventory balance is $8 million and represents 45% of total assets. Management declines to correct the misstatement. What factors should the auditor consider in evaluating whether to require correction?

answers.text: The dollar amount alone is the only relevant consideration — since $185,000 is below the $200,000 tolerable misstatement, no correction is required

The auditor must consider both the quantitative amount (close to tolerable misstatement) and qualitative factors — the overstatement's proximity to tolerable misstatement, its effect on the entity's financial ratios, its interaction with other uncorrected misstatements, and whether the pattern is consistent with management bias
Since management declined to correct it, the auditor has no further recourse and must accept the misstatement
The misstatement should be accepted because inventory at 45% of total assets is always immaterial regardless of its dollar amount

explanations.a: The dollar amount relative to tolerable misstatement is the primary quantitative consideration but not the only factor. When a misstatement approaches tolerable misstatement, the auditor must evaluate whether the aggregate of all uncorrected misstatements — combined with undetected misstatements — could exceed overall materiality.
explanations.b: When management declines to correct a misstatement, the auditor evaluates: (1) the proximity of $185,000 to the $200,000 tolerable misstatement — with only a $15,000 margin, there is limited buffer; (2) the combined effect with other uncorrected misstatements — if other immaterial uncorrected misstatements also exist, the aggregate may approach or exceed performance materiality; (3) qualitative factors — the overstatement of a significant asset (45% of total assets) may affect key financial ratios that users rely on; (4) whether the pattern is consistent with management bias (if management consistently declines to correct overstatements, this pattern may be evidence of intentional misstatement); and (5) whether additional testing is warranted to assess the true magnitude of the misstatement more precisely.
explanations.c: If management declines to correct a misstatement, the auditor's recourse includes: requesting again, explaining the significance; communicating to those charged with governance; if material individually or in aggregate with other uncorrected misstatements, modifying the audit opinion; and potentially considering whether the declination indicates management bias or fraud risk.
explanations.d: The size of an asset relative to total assets determines its qualitative significance but does not determine whether a specific dollar misstatement is material or immaterial. Materiality is about the dollar amount of the misstatement relative to the applicable threshold — not the relative size of the account itself.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response
questions.text: An auditor sets overall materiality at $500,000 and performance materiality at $325,000. During the audit, the auditor identifies the following uncorrected misstatements that management declines to correct: (1) overstatement of revenue: $175,000; (2) understatement of warranty liability: $95,000; and (3) overstatement of a deferred tax asset: $70,000. The aggregate is $340,000. How should the auditor evaluate this situation?

answers.text: Each individual misstatement is below overall materiality ($500,000) — no action is required

The aggregate uncorrected misstatements ($340,000) exceed performance materiality ($325,000) but are below overall materiality ($500,000) — the auditor must communicate the aggregate to management and those charged with governance, request reconsideration of corrections, and consider whether the aggregate (combined with likely undetected misstatements) could exceed overall materiality — potentially requiring additional procedures
The auditor should issue an immediate adverse opinion because uncorrected misstatements always require an adverse opinion
The auditor should lower overall materiality to $300,000 to make the aggregate misstatements material and require correction

explanations.a: Evaluating misstatements only individually — not in aggregate — would understate the audit risk. AU-C 450 requires the auditor to accumulate uncorrected misstatements and evaluate their aggregate effect. When the aggregate ($340,000) exceeds performance materiality ($325,000), action is required even though each individual misstatement is below overall materiality.
explanations.b: This is the correct application of AU-C 320 and 450. The aggregate ($340,000) exceeds performance materiality ($325,000) — a threshold designed to signal when the combined effect of uncorrected misstatements warrants attention. The auditor should: communicate the aggregate to management and request that management correct the misstatements (or at least reconsider); communicate the aggregate to TCWG if management declines; evaluate whether the $340,000 of uncorrected misstatements — combined with misstatements that were not detected (sampling risk) — could approach or exceed overall materiality ($500,000); and consider whether additional testing is needed to obtain greater comfort that undetected misstatements do not push the aggregate above overall materiality. If the auditor concludes the aggregate could be material and management refuses to correct, a modified opinion is considered.
explanations.c: Uncorrected misstatements require evaluation and communication — they do not automatically trigger an adverse opinion. An adverse opinion is issued when misstatements are material AND pervasive. If the aggregate is below overall materiality, an unmodified opinion may still be appropriate after appropriate communication.
explanations.d: The auditor cannot lower overall materiality simply to compel corrections. Materiality is determined based on professional judgment about user information needs — not adjusted downward strategically to force management's hand.
