If the auditor believes the threshold should be lower based on new information, the revision must be based on legitimate professional judgment, not as a negotiation tactic.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response
questions.keyword: assessing and responding to risks of material misstatement
questions.text: At the assertion level, the risk of material misstatement (RMM) consists of which two components?

answers.text: Inherent risk — the susceptibility of an assertion to misstatement before consideration of any controls — and control risk — the risk that a material misstatement would not be prevented, or detected and corrected, by the entity's internal controls
Detection risk and sampling risk, which together determine how likely the auditor is to find misstatements
Audit risk and business risk, which together determine the overall engagement risk
Fraud risk and error risk, which together encompass all potential causes of financial statement misstatement

explanations.a: The risk of material misstatement at the assertion level consists of: (1) inherent risk — the susceptibility of a specific assertion to a misstatement that could be material, assuming no related controls (e.g., fair value measurements have high inherent risk because they are complex and judgmental); and (2) control risk — the risk that a misstatement that could be material will not be prevented, or detected and corrected on a timely basis, by the entity's internal controls. Together, inherent risk and control risk determine the risk that the financial statements contain a material misstatement — before the auditor performs any procedures.
explanations.b: Detection risk is the third component of the audit risk model — it is the risk that the auditor's procedures will not detect a material misstatement that exists. It is not a component of the risk of material misstatement; rather, it is the auditor's risk that results from insufficient audit procedures. Sampling risk is a component of detection risk.
explanations.c: Audit risk is the overall model that encompasses all three components (inherent risk × control risk × detection risk). Business risk is the entity's risk of not achieving its objectives — it informs inherent risk assessment but is not a direct component of RMM as defined in auditing standards.
explanations.d: Fraud risk and error risk are types of misstatement risk by cause — they do not represent the two formal components of RMM at the assertion level. The formal components are inherent risk and control risk.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response
questions.keyword: assessing and responding to risks of material misstatement
questions.text: AU-C Section 315 requires the auditor to identify 'significant risks' — risks that require special audit consideration. Which of the following BEST describes a significant risk?

answers.text: Any account balance that exceeds $1 million regardless of the nature of the transactions it contains
A risk that has been identified in a prior-year audit but was not material in any prior period
A risk that requires the auditor to file an immediate report with the SEC upon identification

A risk of material misstatement at the assertion level that, in the auditor's judgment, requires special audit consideration — typically characterized by high inherent risk from factors such as significant judgment, unusual transactions, complexity, or susceptibility to fraud

explanations.a: Account balance size alone does not define a significant risk. A large account in a routine, well-controlled process may have lower inherent risk than a smaller account involving complex estimates or significant management judgment. Significant risks are defined by the nature and characteristics of the risk, not solely by dollar size.
explanations.b: A risk identified in a prior year is relevant context for current-year planning, but its historical immateriality does not define it as a significant risk. Significant risk designation is based on the current-period assessment of inherent risk characteristics — complex estimates, susceptibility to fraud, unusual transactions, or significant management judgment.
explanations.c: Significant risks do not trigger SEC reporting obligations. Significant risks are a planning and risk assessment concept within the audit — they require special consideration in audit planning and execution, not regulatory reporting.
explanations.d: AU-C Section 315 defines significant risks as risks of material misstatement that require special audit consideration. These are typically identified when the auditor assesses high inherent risk due to: significant management judgment or estimation uncertainty (fair value measurements, revenue recognition in complex arrangements); unusual or non-routine transactions; complex accounting (business combinations, derivatives, foreign currency); or susceptibility to fraud (areas where management has motivation and opportunity to misstate). Significant risks always require substantive procedures specifically designed to address them and cannot be addressed by reliance on controls alone.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response
questions.keyword: assessing and responding to risks of material misstatement
questions.text: When the auditor develops responses to assessed risks of material misstatement, auditing standards require two types of responses. Which statement BEST describes these two types?

answers.text: Responses for public company audits (PCAOB) and responses for private company audits (GAAS), which differ only in the extent of documentation required
Responses to prior-year risks (carried forward from the prior audit) and responses to new risks (first identified in the current year)

Overall responses that address the audit broadly (e.g., more experienced staff, unpredictability, increased supervision) and assertion-level responses that address specific risks for individual accounts and assertions through the nature, timing, and extent of procedures
Preventive responses (designed before misstatements occur) and detective responses (designed to find misstatements after they occur)

explanations.a: While PCAOB and AICPA GAAS have differences in their detailed requirements, the conceptual framework for responding to assessed risks is similar in both — both require overall and assertion-level responses. The distinction is not based on entity type.
explanations.b: The distinction between prior-year and new risks is a risk assessment consideration — not the framework for designing audit responses. Responses are designed based on the assessed level of risk in the current period, regardless of when the risk was first identified.
explanations.c: AU-C Section 330 requires the auditor to design and implement overall responses to address assessed risks at the financial statement level, and specific responses at the assertion level. Overall responses address the audit broadly: assigning more experienced or specialized staff; incorporating more unpredictability into the audit (testing at unexpected times or in unexpected areas); providing heightened supervision; and implementing a general stance of increased skepticism. Assertion-level responses address specific risks for individual accounts and assertions: designing the nature (type of procedure — inspection, confirmation, recalculation), timing (interim versus year-end), and extent (sample sizes, coverage percentages) of procedures responsive to each assessed risk.
explanations.d: Preventive and detective controls are internal control classifications — not categories of audit responses. While audit procedures can be described as designed to detect misstatements, the framework for designing audit responses to assessed risks is not organized around this distinction.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response
questions.keyword: assessing and responding to risks of material misstatement
questions.text: An auditor assesses the valuation assertion for a complex investment portfolio as having high inherent risk due to the use of Level 3 fair value inputs, but also concludes that the entity's controls over the valuation process are effective. How should the auditor design audit procedures for this assertion?

answers.text: Test controls only — since controls are effective, no substantive procedures are required for this assertion
Perform substantive procedures only — since inherent risk is high, controls cannot be relied upon regardless of their assessed effectiveness

Test the controls and if they are found to be operating effectively, use that evidence to reduce the extent of substantive procedures — but still perform substantive procedures specifically designed for the significant risk of high inherent risk in Level 3 valuations
Treat the high inherent risk and effective controls as offsetting factors and apply only standard-level substantive procedures with no modification

explanations.a: Even when controls are effective, substantive procedures cannot be eliminated for significant risks. AU-C 330 explicitly states that for significant risks, the auditor shall perform substantive procedures specifically responsive to the risk — substantive procedures are required regardless of control effectiveness for significant risks.
explanations.b: Effective controls over a complex process provide relevant audit evidence — even for high-inherent-risk areas. The auditor can test controls and, if they are found to be operating effectively, reduce the extent (though not eliminate) substantive procedures. Completely disregarding effective controls would not be an appropriate application of the audit risk model.
explanations.c: This reflects the correct application of AU-C 330 for a significant risk with effective controls. The auditor: (1) tests the controls over the valuation process to confirm they are operating as designed; (2) if control testing confirms effectiveness, uses that as a basis for reducing the extent of substantive procedures (e.g., testing a smaller sample of valuations, relying more heavily on analytical procedures); but (3) because this is a significant risk (high inherent risk from Level 3 inputs), the auditor must still perform substantive procedures specifically designed for this risk — which for complex Level 3 valuations would typically include: engaging a valuation specialist, independently testing key assumptions, challenging the valuation model methodology, and reviewing the appropriateness of inputs.
explanations.d: Simply applying standard-level procedures without modification for a high-inherent-risk significant risk would not constitute an adequate response. The nature, timing, and extent of procedures must be responsive to the assessed level of risk — high inherent risk demands more rigorous or targeted substantive procedures than low-risk areas, even when controls are effective.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response
questions.keyword: assessing and responding to risks of material misstatement
questions.text: An auditor performs substantive procedures on accounts receivable at an interim date (October 31) for a December 31 year-end audit, rather than at year-end. The primary condition that must be met to use an interim date for substantive procedures is

answers.text: Management must agree to prepare additional schedules bridging October 31 to December 31 at no additional cost to the client
The accounts receivable balance must be immaterial at year-end so the rollforward period is unimportant

The auditor must be satisfied that the additional risk created by the two-month gap between the interim testing date and year-end can be appropriately managed through rollforward procedures covering that period
Interim substantive procedures are only permitted for nonissuer audits — issuers must have all substantive procedures performed at year-end

explanations.a: Management's cooperation with interim schedules is a practical consideration but is not the substantive professional standards condition for performing interim substantive procedures. The primary condition relates to the additional risk created by the timing gap and whether it can be adequately managed.
explanations.b: The immateriality of the balance at year-end would eliminate the need for substantive procedures entirely — not be a condition for testing at an interim date. Interim substantive procedures are used for material accounts where the timing can be moved for efficiency while still maintaining adequate coverage.
explanations.c: AU-C Section 330 provides that the auditor may perform substantive procedures at an interim date when: the auditor can manage the additional risk created by the gap between the interim testing date and year-end. Managing this risk requires: (1) designing rollforward procedures (additional testing of transactions occurring between the interim date and year-end to confirm the year-end balance is reliable); (2) assessing whether the control environment is sufficiently strong to provide assurance that significant misstatements would not arise between October 31 and December 31; and (3) considering whether there are significant transactions, events, or risks in the remaining period that warrant year-end testing. If these conditions can be met, interim substantive testing is permissible.
explanations.d: There is no prohibition on interim substantive procedures for issuer audits under PCAOB standards. Both PCAOB and AICPA standards permit substantive procedures at interim dates, subject to appropriate rollforward coverage. Issuers are subject to additional integrated audit requirements (ICFR), but interim substantive procedures are not prohibited.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response
questions.keyword: assessing and responding to risks of material misstatement
questions.text: When assessing the risk of material misstatement at the assertion level for the existence assertion in inventory, an auditor would focus on which factors?

answers.text: The entity's revenue recognition policy — because revenue recognition drives the timing of when inventory is removed from the balance sheet
Whether the accounts payable balance is properly stated — because payables and inventory are always recorded together in the same transaction
The completeness of inventory disclosures in the notes to the financial statements

The reliability of the perpetual inventory system, the frequency and results of cycle counts, the physical security of inventory locations, and the history of inventory adjustments — factors that determine whether recorded inventory actually exists

explanations.a: Revenue recognition affects when inventory is relieved from the balance sheet (cost of goods sold), but the existence assertion — whether recorded inventory physically exists at the reporting date — is more directly affected by the physical controls, recordkeeping, and count procedures surrounding inventory rather than the revenue recognition policy.
explanations.b: Accounts payable and inventory are related in the purchasing cycle, but the existence assertion for inventory focuses on whether the inventory that appears in the records is actually present — not on the payable side of the transaction. A payable misstatement would be assessed under the completeness assertion for liabilities, not the existence assertion for inventory.
explanations.c: Disclosure completeness in the notes is relevant to the presentation and disclosure assertion — not the existence assertion. The existence assertion asks whether the recorded inventory physically exists; completeness of disclosures is a different assertion addressing whether required information about inventory is disclosed.
explanations.d: The existence assertion for inventory asks: does the inventory that is recorded on the books actually exist? The factors that influence inherent risk for this assertion include: the reliability of the perpetual inventory system (whether the records accurately track physical movements); the frequency and results of physical inventory counts and cycle counts (whether count procedures are effective at detecting discrepancies); physical security of inventory locations (whether unauthorized access or theft is deterred); and the history of inventory adjustments (whether prior counts have revealed significant unexplained differences). These factors collectively determine how susceptible the recorded inventory balance is to including items that do not physically exist.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response
questions.keyword: assessing and responding to risks of material misstatement
questions.text: An auditor assesses goodwill impairment testing as having high inherent risk — the test involves complex discounted cash flow models, significant management judgment about growth rates and discount rates, and a history of management's estimates being optimistic relative to actual outcomes. Controls over the impairment testing process are also assessed as ineffective. Considering both components of RMM, which audit response is MOST appropriate?

answers.text: Rely on management's written representations confirming that goodwill is not impaired, supplemented by a review of the prior-year impairment test

Design comprehensive substantive procedures specifically responsive to the significant risk — including engaging a valuation specialist to independently assess the DCF model, testing key assumptions for reasonableness against external data, reviewing the pattern of prior estimation bias, and applying heightened professional skepticism throughout
Issue a qualified opinion because the combination of high inherent risk and ineffective controls always results in a scope limitation
Perform tests of controls to confirm they are ineffective, then use that result as the basis for issuing a going concern opinion

explanations.a: Management's written representations are insufficient evidence for a significant risk area with high inherent risk and ineffective controls. The combination of subjective estimates, complex models, and management's history of optimistic estimates makes independent verification essential — not management's self-assessment. Prior-year review alone would not address the current-year risk.
explanations.b: When both inherent risk and control risk are high, the combined RMM is at its maximum level. The audit response must be comprehensive and specifically designed to address the identified risk factors: (1) a valuation specialist provides independent expertise in DCF methodology that the audit team may lack, enabling assessment of model structure, discount rate appropriateness, and reasonableness of long-term growth assumptions; (2) testing key assumptions against external data (industry growth forecasts, market discount rates, comparable company multiples) provides objective corroboration or contradicts management's assumptions; (3) retrospective review of prior estimates versus actual outcomes quantifies the historical bias pattern, informing how much skepticism to apply to current-year estimates; (4) heightened professional skepticism means challenging rather than accepting management's conclusions, exploring downside scenarios, and evaluating whether the impairment model is appropriately sensitive to adverse changes in key assumptions. This is the type of comprehensive, risk-responsive substantive approach required by AU-C 330 for significant risks.
explanations.c: High RMM does not automatically result in a scope limitation or qualified opinion. High RMM means the auditor must perform more extensive and carefully designed procedures — but those procedures, if properly designed and executed, provide sufficient evidence to support an opinion. A scope limitation arises when the auditor cannot obtain sufficient evidence, not when the risk assessment is high.
explanations.d: Confirming ineffective controls is a risk assessment finding — it affects how much reliance can be placed on controls and therefore the extent of substantive testing required. It does not lead directly to a going concern opinion. Going concern is an assessment of the entity's ability to continue operations for the foreseeable future — it is not a response to high RMM in a specific account area.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response
questions.keyword: planning for and using work of others
questions.text: When an external auditor uses the work of an internal audit function or an auditor's specialist, responsibility for the audit opinion

answers.text: Remains solely with the external auditor — using others' work does not transfer or reduce the external auditor's responsibility for the opinion
Is shared equally between the external auditor and the specialist or internal auditors whose work was used
Transfers to the specialist or internal auditor for the specific area in which their work was used
Is eliminated for areas covered by internal auditors since their work replaces the external auditor's procedures in those areas

explanations.a: AU-C Sections 610 and 620 are clear that using the work of internal auditors or an auditor's specialist does not reduce the external auditor's sole responsibility for the audit opinion. The external auditor remains the responsible party — their judgment about the sufficiency and appropriateness of evidence must drive every conclusion, including in areas where others' work was used. This responsibility cannot be delegated or shared.
explanations.b: Responsibility for the audit opinion is not shared — it rests entirely with the external auditor. The internal auditors and specialists provide assistance and evidence, but they are not co-responsible for the opinion. Their work must be evaluated and supervised by the external auditor.
explanations.c: Responsibility does not transfer to specialists or internal auditors for any portion of the audit. The external auditor evaluates the work of others and determines whether it provides sufficient appropriate evidence — but the conclusion and the opinion remain the external auditor's.
explanations.d: Internal auditors' work supplements the external auditor's procedures — it does not replace them. Even when internal audit work is used extensively, the external auditor must evaluate its quality and may need to perform additional procedures to obtain sufficient evidence.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response
questions.keyword: planning for and using work of others
questions.text: Before relying on the work of an entity's internal audit function, the external auditor must evaluate which factors?

answers.text: The internal auditors' salary levels and years of experience within the company
Whether internal audit members have passed the CIA exam and maintain continuing professional education

The internal audit function's organizational status and objectivity, the technical competence of its members, and whether the function applies a systematic and disciplined approach — including quality control
Whether the internal audit department's budget was approved by the board of directors

explanations.a: Salary levels and years of tenure are not the relevant evaluative factors under AU-C 610. What matters is whether the internal auditors have the competence and objectivity necessary to produce reliable work — not their compensation.
explanations.b: CIA certification may be evidence of competence, but it is not required. AU-C 610 does not mandate specific professional credentials — the evaluation focuses on demonstrated competence through training, experience, and professional standards, not specific certifications.
explanations.c: AU-C Section 610 requires the external auditor to evaluate three key factors before using internal audit work: (1) organizational status and objectivity — whether internal audit reports to a sufficiently high level and has freedom from management interference in planning and reporting (e.g., reporting to the audit committee); (2) technical competence — whether internal auditors possess the skills, training, and experience needed to perform the relevant procedures; and (3) systematic and disciplined approach — whether the function applies professional standards and has quality control procedures that ensure the reliability of its work product.
explanations.d: Board approval of the internal audit budget is an element of governance — it is relevant to understanding whether the function has adequate resources, but it is not one of the three primary factors that the external auditor is required to evaluate under AU-C 610.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response
questions.keyword: planning for and using work of others
questions.text: When internal auditors provide direct assistance — performing audit procedures under the external auditor's direct supervision — the external auditor's obligations include

answers.text: Issuing a joint audit report co-signed by both the external auditor and the internal audit director

Directing, supervising, and reviewing the work of the internal auditors, and evaluating whether their work was properly planned and executed — applying the same quality standards as for external audit team members
Registering the internal auditors with the PCAOB before they can perform any procedures on issuer engagements
Obtaining the audit committee's written pre-approval for each specific procedure performed by internal auditors

explanations.a: A joint audit report is not required or standard when internal auditors provide direct assistance. The external auditor issues the audit report solely — the participation of internal auditors is not disclosed in the report (with the exception of PCAOB standards for issuers, which limit or prohibit direct assistance in certain circumstances).
explanations.b: AU-C Section 610 requires that when internal auditors provide direct assistance (performing audit procedures under the external auditor's direction), the external auditor must: provide direction and supervision to the internal auditors performing those procedures; review the work product of those procedures to ensure it meets the external auditor's quality standards; and evaluate whether the work was adequately planned and executed. The external auditor must also assess the risk that internal auditors may not maintain the independence or objectivity needed for the tasks assigned.
explanations.c: PCAOB registration applies to accounting firms registered with the PCAOB — not to an entity's internal audit staff. Internal auditors providing assistance on external audits do not register with the PCAOB; they work under the supervision of the registered external audit firm.
explanations.d: Audit committee pre-approval for each specific procedure performed by internal auditors is not required. The audit committee's oversight of the external auditor's overall approach (including the use of internal auditors in certain roles) may be communicated as part of the planned scope, but procedure-by-procedure approval is not mandated.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response
questions.keyword: planning for and using work of others
questions.text: An entity uses a management's specialist (a certified actuarial firm) to calculate its defined benefit pension obligation. The external auditor engages a separate valuation specialist to evaluate the actuarial calculations. In this scenario, the external auditor's specialist is BEST described as

answers.text: An agent of management, since they are working on the same subject matter as management's specialist
A replacement for management's specialist — once the external auditor's specialist is engaged, management's specialist's work is disregarded

An auditor's specialist — an independent expert whose work is used by the external auditor as audit evidence, and whose competence, capability, and objectivity must be evaluated before relying on their work
A co-signer of the audit report, since their specialized conclusions form the basis for the auditor's opinion on the pension obligation

explanations.a: The external auditor's specialist is engaged by and works for the external auditor — they are not an agent of management. Their independence from management is a key factor the external auditor evaluates before relying on their work.
explanations.b: The external auditor's specialist's work does not replace management's specialist's work — it provides an independent evaluation of the reasonableness of management's actuarial calculations. Both analyses inform the external auditor's assessment, with the auditor's specialist providing independent corroboration or challenge to management's estimates.
explanations.c: AU-C Section 620 defines an auditor's specialist as an individual or organization with expertise in a field other than accounting or auditing whose work assists the auditor. Before relying on an auditor's specialist, the external auditor must evaluate their professional competence (qualifications, experience, professional standing), capability (available resources), and objectivity (independence from the entity and management). The auditor's specialist is engaged by the external auditor, not by management — this distinguishes them from a management's specialist.
explanations.d: The auditor's specialist does not co-sign the audit report. Their work is used as audit evidence by the external auditor, who then forms their own independent opinion. The responsibility for the audit opinion remains solely with the external auditor.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response
questions.keyword: planning for and using work of others
questions.text: An internal audit function has been assessed as highly competent, independent, and systematic. The external auditor is planning to use internal audit work in three areas: (1) testing of routine accounts payable transactions; (2) evaluating management's goodwill impairment assessment; and (3) testing revenue recognition for the entity's only revenue stream, which was identified as a fraud risk area. For which area(s) should the external auditor be MOST cautious about relying on internal audit work?

answers.text: Area 1 only — routine accounts payable testing is the highest risk area because it involves cash disbursements

Areas 2 and 3 — the auditor should be cautious about relying on internal audit work for significant judgment areas and fraud risk areas, even if the internal audit function is assessed as competent and independent
None of the areas require caution since the internal audit function has been positively assessed in all three evaluation criteria
Area 3 only — goodwill impairment is a routine estimate that internal auditors can test reliably

explanations.a: Routine accounts payable testing (Area 1) is a lower-risk area that is generally appropriate for external auditors to use internal audit work — the transactions are routine, well-controlled, and the risk of material misstatement from fraud or significant judgment is lower.
explanations.b: AU-C Section 610 limits the extent to which external auditors can use internal audit work based on risk: (1) for higher-risk areas involving significant auditor judgment — such as goodwill impairment assessments (Area 2) that require complex estimates and specialist-level evaluation — the external auditor should perform more of the work directly; and (2) for identified fraud risk areas (Area 3) — revenue recognized as a fraud risk — the external auditor should not rely on internal audit work, because fraud risk areas require the external auditor's own independent professional skepticism and procedures. A positive overall assessment of the internal audit function does not override these specific limitations for high-judgment and fraud-risk areas.
explanations.c: A positive overall assessment of the internal audit function does not mean the external auditor can rely on internal audit work without limitation in all areas. AU-C 610 specifically identifies higher-risk and fraud-risk areas as places where external auditor involvement must be greater, regardless of internal audit quality.
explanations.d: Goodwill impairment assessment (Area 2) is not a routine estimate — it involves complex discounted cash flow models, significant management judgment, and specialized valuation expertise. It is specifically the type of higher-risk, judgment-intensive area where external auditor caution about relying on internal audit work is required.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response
questions.text: AU-C Section 250 distinguishes between two categories of laws and regulations relevant to the auditor's responsibilities. Which statement BEST describes these two categories?

answers.text: International laws and domestic laws — the auditor has greater responsibility for compliance with domestic law
Federal laws and state laws — the auditor must address federal compliance in every audit but state compliance only in some jurisdictions
Criminal laws and civil laws — the auditor must report criminal violations to law enforcement but only discloses civil violations in the notes

Laws with direct effect on material amounts in the financial statements (e.g., tax, ERISA, SEC reporting) where the auditor has greater responsibility — and laws with only indirect effect (e.g., environmental, employment safety) where the auditor's responsibility is more limited

explanations.a: The distinction between international and domestic law is not the framework used in AU-C 250. The standard's framework is based on the nature of the law's effect on the financial statements — direct versus indirect — not on the source jurisdiction.
explanations.b: Federal versus state law is not the organizing framework of AU-C 250. Both federal and state laws can have direct effects on financial statement amounts, and the auditor's responsibilities are determined by the nature of the law's effect on financial reporting — not by which level of government enacted it.
explanations.c: Criminal versus civil law classification is not the framework in AU-C 250. The auditor's reporting obligations for illegal acts depend on factors including the impact on the financial statements and the auditor's engagement type — not solely on whether a violation is criminal or civil.
explanations.d: AU-C Section 250 establishes two categories with different auditor responsibilities: (1) Laws and regulations having direct effect on material amounts in the financial statements — such as income tax laws (affect tax provisions), ERISA (affects pension obligations), and SEC reporting requirements (affect disclosures) — where the auditor is responsible for designing audit procedures to detect material misstatements from noncompliance; and (2) Other laws and regulations where noncompliance may have a financial statement effect but the primary effect is operational (environmental regulations, workplace safety laws, data privacy laws) — where the auditor designs procedures to identify material misstatements from noncompliance but is not expected to proactively search for compliance violations.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response
questions.text: During an audit, an auditor obtains evidence suggesting that the entity may have violated the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act (FCPA) by making improper payments to government officials in connection with winning a foreign government contract. The auditor's MOST appropriate immediate response is to

answers.text: Include a qualified opinion in the audit report specifically identifying the FCPA violation

Communicate the matter to the appropriate level of management and those charged with governance, evaluate whether the financial effects are properly reflected and disclosed, and consider the implications for the audit and for management's representations
Contact the SEC and DOJ immediately to report the violation before informing management
Disregard the matter since international bribery laws are outside the scope of financial statement audits

explanations.a: Issuing a qualified opinion immediately based on a potential violation is premature. The auditor must first understand the nature and extent of the potential violation, whether it has been properly accounted for and disclosed, and what management plans to do about it — before determining the effect on the audit opinion.
explanations.b: AU-C Section 250 requires the auditor, upon identifying or suspecting noncompliance with laws, to: (1) communicate with the appropriate level of management (and those charged with governance if senior management is involved or if the matter is significant); (2) evaluate the financial statement implications — including whether the potential liability, fines, or penalties have been properly accrued and disclosed; (3) consider the effect on the reliability of management's representations; and (4) determine whether additional audit procedures are needed to understand the full scope of the issue.
explanations.c: Immediately contacting regulatory authorities before informing management and TCWG is not the auditor's first required action under AU-C 250. The auditor's primary communication obligations run to management and TCWG. Regulatory reporting by the external auditor is generally not required in most circumstances — with limited exceptions (e.g., certain specific regulatory frameworks, or when management and TCWG fail to take appropriate remedial action and the matter involves the auditor's own report).
explanations.d: The FCPA (Foreign Corrupt Practices Act) is a U.S. law directly applicable to U.S. companies and their foreign operations. Violations can result in significant monetary penalties and reputational consequences that must be disclosed in the financial statements. FCPA compliance is directly within the scope of the auditor's consideration of laws with potential direct financial statement effects.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response
questions.text: An auditor identifies that an entity has violated OSHA workplace safety regulations during the year, resulting in a significant penalty that was not recorded. The violation occurred in manufacturing operations that are not directly connected to the financial reporting process. How should the auditor evaluate this situation?

answers.text: Evaluate whether the unrecorded penalty creates a material misstatement in the financial statements — if material, the penalty must be properly accrued or disclosed; the fact that OSHA is an indirect-effect law does not eliminate the financial statement impact of a material unrecorded liability
Ignore the violation since OSHA regulations are in the category of laws with only indirect financial statement effects, which are outside the auditor's scope
Report the OSHA violation to the Department of Labor before completing the audit, as required by AU-C 250
Immediately withdraw from the engagement because safety violations indicate management's lack of integrity in all areas

explanations.a: While OSHA is generally classified as a law with indirect rather than direct effect on financial statement amounts (OSHA regulations govern workplace safety, not accounting), the financial consequence of a violation — a significant penalty — can directly affect the financial statements through an unrecorded liability. The auditor must evaluate: (1) whether the penalty is material to the financial statements; (2) whether a liability has been properly accrued and measured; (3) whether required contingency disclosures have been made; and (4) whether additional penalties, fines, or remediation costs may be incurred. The classification of OSHA as an indirect-effect law affects what proactive search procedures the auditor performs — it does not eliminate the auditor's responsibility for material misstatements that arise from noncompliance.
explanations.b: Classifying OSHA as an indirect-effect law does not mean the auditor ignores its financial consequences. AU-C 250 identifies indirect-effect laws as those where the auditor is less actively searching for compliance violations — but when a violation and its associated penalty come to the auditor's attention, the auditor must evaluate the financial statement impact regardless of which category the law falls into.
explanations.c: AU-C 250 does not require auditors to proactively report workplace safety violations to the Department of Labor. The auditor's primary obligations are to management and TCWG, with very limited exceptions for regulatory reporting that are not triggered by an OSHA penalty.
explanations.d: A single regulatory violation, while serious, does not automatically indicate pervasive management integrity failures or require immediate withdrawal. The auditor must evaluate the specific facts and circumstances — including whether the violation was intentional or negligent, how management responds, and whether it reflects broader control or integrity issues — before determining any effect on the engagement.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response
questions.text: During an audit, an auditor discovers strong evidence that the entity has been falsely certifying compliance with federal grant requirements — receiving federal funds for program activities that were not actually performed. Management acknowledges the issue but declines to take remedial action. Those charged with governance have been informed but have also declined to act. Which response reflects the MOST appropriate course of action under professional standards?

answers.text: Continue the audit and issue an unmodified opinion since the noncompliance with grant requirements does not affect the general purpose financial statements
Expand testing of the grant program in the following year to monitor whether the behavior continues before taking any action in the current year

Consider withdrawing from the engagement and communicating the reasons for withdrawal to those charged with governance; the auditor may also need to consider whether there is an obligation to notify regulatory or funding agencies or other authorities outside the entity
Issue a disclaimer of opinion covering only the grant-funded activities, leaving the financial statement opinion unmodified

explanations.a: Continuing with an unmodified opinion when management and TCWG have declined to address evidence of material fraudulent claims against the federal government is not appropriate. False certification of compliance with federal grant requirements likely involves intentional misrepresentation — a form of fraud — that has significant legal and financial implications that must be addressed in the audit.
explanations.b: Deferring action to a future year's audit when the auditor has identified what appears to be ongoing fraudulent activity in the current year leaves the current-year financial statements potentially misstated and fails the auditor's professional responsibility to respond appropriately to identified fraud.
explanations.c: AU-C Section 250 and AU-C 240 establish that when the auditor identifies material noncompliance — particularly noncompliance involving intentional deception — and management and TCWG fail to take appropriate remedial action, the auditor should consider withdrawing from the engagement and explaining the reasons to TCWG. Additionally, where the entity receives federal funding and the auditor identifies fraudulent misrepresentation of compliance with grant requirements, the auditor may have obligations to consider whether reporting to funding agencies, oversight bodies, or other regulatory authorities is appropriate — particularly in the context of a single audit, where the auditor has specific reporting responsibilities regarding compliance with federal program requirements.
explanations.d: A disclaimer of opinion covering only specific activity is not a standard audit report modification option under US GAAS. The standard modification options (qualified, adverse, disclaimer of opinion) apply to the financial statements as a whole or to specific matters that affect the overall opinion — not to carved-out portions of activity.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response
questions.text: Which of the following represents an accounting estimate that requires auditor attention?

answers.text: The face value of bonds payable issued at par with no discount or premium
The amount of cash and cash equivalents per the bank statement reconciled by the entity
Recorded inventory at purchase cost for items not yet sold from the prior quarter
The allowance for doubtful accounts, warranty reserve, goodwill impairment assessment, and fair value of Level 3 financial instruments

explanations.a: Bonds payable issued at par with no discount or premium represent a known contractual amount — there is no estimation involved. The face value is fixed by the bond indenture and does not require management judgment about uncertain future amounts.
explanations.b: Cash and cash equivalents reconciled to the bank statement are verified amounts — the balance is determined by counting and reconciling to objective third-party records, not by estimating uncertain future amounts.
explanations.c: Inventory recorded at purchase cost is a historical transaction amount — no estimation is required for inventory held at cost below market. Estimation would be required for lower of cost or net realizable value adjustments (e.g., obsolescence reserves), not for the cost of items not yet sold.
explanations.d: AU-C Section 540 defines accounting estimates as approximations of monetary amounts when there is no precise means of measurement. The allowance for doubtful accounts requires estimating future collection rates; the warranty reserve requires estimating future claim rates and costs; goodwill impairment requires estimating future cash flows and discount rates; and Level 3 fair value instruments require estimating values without observable market prices. All four involve significant management judgment about uncertain future amounts.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response
questions.text: During planning, an auditor identifies that an entity's deferred revenue estimate for unfulfilled subscription obligations involves significant management judgment about customer cancellation rates and expected service delivery timing. Which factor would MOST indicate that this estimate has HIGH estimation uncertainty?

answers.text: The estimate has been prepared using the same methodology as the prior year without changes
The estimate is immaterial to the financial statements as a whole
Independent market data is available to benchmark the cancellation rate assumptions
The estimate is highly sensitive to small changes in assumed cancellation rates — a 2% change in cancellation rate assumptions produces a 35% change in the estimated liability

explanations.a: Consistency with prior-year methodology does not indicate high estimation uncertainty — it may actually indicate lower uncertainty if the prior methodology has been validated by comparison to actual outcomes. A stable, well-established methodology tends to reduce (not increase) estimation uncertainty.
explanations.b: Immateriality reduces the audit significance of estimation uncertainty. If the estimate is immaterial, even high uncertainty does not create a significant audit risk for the financial statements as a whole.
explanations.c: The availability of independent market data to benchmark assumptions reduces estimation uncertainty — the auditor can corroborate management's assumptions against observable data. High estimation uncertainty typically arises when such data is absent (Level 3 inputs).
explanations.d: AU-C Section 540 identifies sensitivity to changes in assumptions as a key indicator of high estimation uncertainty. When small changes in an assumption produce large changes in the estimated amount — such as a 2% change in cancellation rates producing a 35% change in the liability — the estimate is highly sensitive and therefore highly uncertain. This sensitivity means that management's choice of assumption has enormous financial statement impact, and the reasonableness of that assumption is critical to the fair presentation of the statements.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response
questions.text: During planning, an auditor identifies accounting estimates that will require attention during the audit. Which of the following procedures is MOST useful for identifying accounting estimates in a new audit engagement?

answers.text: Reviewing the prior auditor's workpapers for estimates that were identified in prior periods
Requesting that management identify all items in the financial statements that do not require estimation

Reviewing the entity's accounting policies and prior-period financial statements, inquiring of management about new estimates in the current period, and understanding the entity's business processes to identify areas requiring significant judgment
Relying entirely on the prior-year auditor's risk assessment memo since accounting estimates rarely change between years

explanations.a: Reviewing prior-year workpapers is one useful source of information but is insufficient alone — especially if the entity has new activities, changed business conditions, or adopted new accounting standards that create new estimates. The prior-year workpapers also cover only estimates that existed in prior periods, not any new ones that may have arisen.
explanations.b: Requesting that management identify non-estimate items is an indirect approach that may not work effectively — management might not accurately classify all items. A more direct approach is to positively identify all items that do require estimation through review of the financial statements and business processes.
explanations.c: The most comprehensive approach to identifying accounting estimates during planning combines multiple sources: (1) reviewing accounting policies to understand where the entity applies estimation in its accounting (revenue recognition, depreciation, allowances, fair values); (2) reviewing prior-period financial statements to identify estimates already in use; (3) inquiring of management about any new estimates arising from new transactions, new accounting standards, or changed business conditions in the current period; and (4) understanding business processes to identify areas where judgment is inherent (e.g., a construction company will have contract completion estimates; a financial institution will have credit loss reserves).
explanations.d: Prior-year risk assessments are a useful starting point but cannot be relied upon entirely. Business conditions, market environments, accounting standard changes, and entity-specific changes (new products, acquisitions) regularly create new estimation areas or significantly change the nature of existing estimates.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response
questions.text: An auditor identifies that an entity's allowance for credit losses (ACL) under CECL has high estimation uncertainty — driven by economic forecasts, portfolio composition, and loan-specific characteristics. In planning audit procedures for this estimate, the auditor should focus on which aspects?

answers.text: Evaluating management's process for developing the ACL, assessing the reasonableness of the economic forecasts and model assumptions, testing data inputs for accuracy, and considering whether an independently developed estimate is needed to evaluate management's estimate
Confirming the balance with the external credit rating agency that provided ratings for the entity's loan portfolio
Accepting management's CECL model without testing since it was purchased from a third-party vendor and is presumed to be accurate
Testing only the mathematical accuracy of the CECL model calculations, since the model inputs are provided by management and cannot be independently verified

explanations.a: AU-C Section 540 provides three approaches to auditing accounting estimates: (1) evaluate management's process — including the quality of the process, the reasonableness of the assumptions, and the accuracy of the inputs; (2) develop an independent estimate and compare to management's estimate; (3) review subsequent events that corroborate (or contradict) the estimate. For a CECL allowance with high estimation uncertainty, the auditor should evaluate management's process (the CECL model structure, the economic forecast sources, the segmentation approach), assess whether key assumptions (loss rates, recovery rates, macroeconomic forecast scenarios) are reasonable and supported, test data inputs for accuracy (loan characteristics, historical performance data), and consider whether an independently developed point estimate or range is needed to evaluate the reasonableness of management's conclusion.
explanations.b: External credit rating agencies rate the entity's debt obligations — they do not provide independent verification of the entity's own estimate of credit losses on its loan portfolio. A third-party credit rating is not a substitute for testing management's allowance estimate.
explanations.c: Third-party purchased models are not inherently accurate simply because they come from outside vendors — management's application of the model, the inputs used, and the calibration of the model to the entity's specific portfolio are all subject to management judgment and potential error. The source of the model does not substitute for audit testing of its application.
explanations.d: Mathematical accuracy is one component of testing, but it is insufficient for a high-estimation-uncertainty estimate. If the inputs are wrong — due to classification errors, stale data, or management bias — a mathematically correct calculation will still produce an incorrect estimate. The auditor must test data inputs for accuracy and evaluate the reasonableness of the assumptions, not just verify the arithmetic.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response
questions.text: An auditor performs a retrospective review of prior-period accounting estimates by comparing management's estimates from the prior year to actual outcomes in the current year. This procedure is MOST useful for

answers.text: Determining the exact dollar amount of the current-year estimate without performing additional procedures
Providing evidence for the completeness assertion in accounts receivable — the major area where estimates affect the balance sheet
Replacing the need to evaluate management's current-year estimation process since the retrospective review covers prior-year estimates
Identifying management bias in the estimation process — a consistent pattern of estimates that favor overstating assets or income suggests that current-year estimates may also be biased

explanations.a: A retrospective review does not determine the current-year estimate — it evaluates the reliability of management's prior estimates by comparing them to what actually happened. The current-year estimate still requires its own set of audit procedures.
explanations.b: Accounts receivable completeness is not the primary assertion addressed by retrospective reviews of estimates. The retrospective review addresses the valuation assertion (through allowance estimates) and provides evidence about management bias across all estimation areas — not specifically about whether all receivables have been recorded.
explanations.c: The retrospective review is a planning and evidence procedure — it does not replace the auditor's evaluation of the current-year estimation process. It supplements current-year procedures by providing historical evidence about the reliability of management's estimation approach.
explanations.d: This is the primary purpose of the retrospective review. AU-C Section 540 requires the auditor to review prior-period estimates and compare them to outcomes as a way of: (1) identifying whether management has a history of biased estimation (consistently optimistic loss assumptions, consistently aggressive revenue deferral estimates, etc.); (2) providing context for evaluating current-year estimates; and (3) informing the auditor's skepticism about management's current-period assumptions if a pattern of favorable bias is identified.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response
questions.keyword: related parties and related party transactions
questions.text: Related-party transactions require special audit consideration primarily because

answers.text: Related parties are always trying to manipulate financial statements, making their transactions inherently fraudulent
Related-party transactions always involve amounts that exceed materiality thresholds

Related-party transactions lack the arm's-length presumption of market transactions — they may be priced at non-market terms, may lack independent business rationale, and create disclosure obligations that must be evaluated
Related-party transactions must be eliminated from the financial statements since they do not represent real economic activity

explanations.a: Not all related-party transactions involve manipulation or fraud. Many are legitimate business transactions — for example, a company leasing office space from its parent company may be priced at fair market value with appropriate disclosure. The concern is the potential for non-arm's-length terms, not an assumption of fraud.
explanations.b: Related-party transactions do not always exceed materiality thresholds. They may be any size — from immaterial individual transactions to those that significantly affect the financial statements. Their significance is determined by their nature and required disclosures, not necessarily by their dollar amount.
explanations.c: AU-C Section 550 emphasizes that related-party transactions lack the arm's-length characteristic of transactions between independent parties. When two parties have a relationship that could create a conflict of interest (common ownership, family relationships, management positions in both entities), the transaction terms may be set to benefit one party at the expense of the other — rather than reflecting fair market value. Additionally, ASC 850 (GAAP) requires specific disclosures about the nature of the relationship, the description of the transaction, and the amounts involved — so that users can assess whether related-party relationships have affected the reported results.
explanations.d: Related-party transactions are not eliminated from the financial statements in standalone financial statements — they are disclosed. Elimination occurs in consolidated financial statements where intercompany transactions between the parent and subsidiaries are removed. In standalone statements, related-party transactions are reported and disclosed, not eliminated.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response
questions.keyword: related parties and related party transactions
questions.text: During planning, the auditor performs procedures to identify related parties. Which of the following is a PRIMARY procedure for this purpose?

answers.text: Inquiring of management to obtain a listing of all known related parties and related-party relationships, and reviewing prior-period workpapers, regulatory filings, and significant contracts for previously identified related parties
Performing a physical inspection of the entity's facilities to identify any signage or branding that might suggest related-party ownership
Confirming the identity of all related parties directly with the entity's external legal counsel
Requesting that the entity's customers and suppliers disclose any ownership interests in the entity

explanations.a: AU-C Section 550 requires the auditor to perform procedures to identify related parties and related-party relationships. Primary procedures include: (1) inquiring of management to obtain a complete listing of related parties and the nature of their relationships; (2) reviewing prior-period workpapers for previously identified related parties; (3) reviewing regulatory filings (10-K proxy statements for public companies, annual reports) which require disclosure of related-party relationships; (4) reviewing minutes of meetings of those charged with governance; (5) reviewing significant contracts and other legal documents; and (6) reviewing accounting records for large or unusual transactions that might indicate related-party activity.
explanations.b: Physical inspection of facilities is a useful audit procedure for certain assertions (existence of assets) but is not a primary procedure for identifying related parties. Related-party relationships are identified through documentation review, inquiry, and information analysis — not facility inspections.
explanations.c: Confirming with external legal counsel is useful for identifying litigation and contingencies (AU-C 501), but it is not the primary procedure for identifying related parties. Management and governance records are the primary sources.
explanations.d: Confirming related-party ownership with customers and suppliers is not a standard procedure for related-party identification. Customers and suppliers generally do not have visibility into the ownership structure of their trading partners, and this approach would be impractical and unreliable as a primary identification procedure.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response
questions.keyword: related parties and related party transactions
questions.text: An entity sold commercial real estate to an entity controlled by the CEO's brother for $15 million, which management states is the fair market value. The auditor is evaluating the business purpose and economic substance of this transaction. Which procedure would MOST directly address the risk that the transaction was not conducted at arm's length?

answers.text: Confirm the transaction details with the entity's external legal counsel who reviewed the purchase agreement
Inquire of the CEO whether his brother paid the $15 million in cash or through financing
Review the disclosure in the financial statements to confirm that the related-party relationship and transaction terms have been properly disclosed

Obtain an independent appraisal or review comparable market transactions to evaluate whether $15 million represents fair market value, and assess whether the terms of the transaction (payment terms, conditions) are consistent with what would be expected in an arm's-length transaction

explanations.a: Legal counsel's review confirms that the transaction was properly documented and legally executed — but legal documentation does not establish that the price was fair market value or that the transaction was conducted at arm's length. A legally proper transaction can still involve non-market pricing between related parties.
explanations.b: The form of payment (cash versus financing) does not address whether the price represents fair market value. Whether the CEO's brother paid in cash or through financing is a financial structure question, not an arm's-length pricing evaluation.
explanations.c: Reviewing the disclosure confirms whether the related-party relationship and transaction have been disclosed as required — but it does not evaluate whether the disclosed transaction was conducted at market terms. Proper disclosure of a non-arm's-length transaction does not make the transaction's price fair.
explanations.d: The primary concern with related-party real estate transactions is whether the price represents fair market value — a price that independent third parties would agree to. To evaluate this, the auditor should: obtain an independent appraisal of the property (or evaluate whether management's appraisal used by management meets independence and quality standards); compare the $15 million to market prices for comparable commercial real estate in the area; and review the transaction terms (conditions, contingencies, payment terms) for consistency with what would be expected in an arm's-length market transaction. This is the only procedure that directly addresses whether the price was at market rates.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response
questions.keyword: related parties and related party transactions
questions.text: During testing, an auditor discovers a material revenue transaction with a customer that was not included on management's list of related parties. Investigation reveals the customer is a company controlled by the entity's controller. How should the auditor evaluate this finding?

answers.text: Accept management's explanation that the controller's ownership was inadvertently omitted and add the party to the related-party list without further action

Treat it as a significant finding requiring investigation of the transaction's terms, evaluation of whether the failure to disclose was intentional, reassessment of fraud risk, and consideration of whether other related-party transactions may also have been omitted from management's disclosures
Issue a qualified opinion solely based on the discovery of the undisclosed related party, without performing additional procedures
Assume the omission is immaterial since it was discovered during testing of only one transaction

explanations.a: An undisclosed related-party transaction involving a senior employee (the controller) cannot simply be accepted as an inadvertent omission without investigation. The controller is responsible for financial reporting — the failure to disclose a material relationship involving their own ownership is a significant finding that raises questions about the completeness and accuracy of all related-party disclosures.
explanations.b: AU-C Section 550 specifically addresses the discovery of related-party transactions not previously disclosed by management. When this occurs, the auditor must: (1) investigate the transaction — evaluate its terms, price, and business rationale to determine whether it was at arm's length; (2) evaluate whether the failure to disclose was intentional or inadvertent — an intentional omission by the controller is a significant fraud risk indicator; (3) reassess fraud risk given the new information about management's completeness of disclosures; (4) perform additional procedures to assess whether other undisclosed related-party transactions may exist; and (5) communicate the matter to those charged with governance.
explanations.c: Issuing a qualified opinion based solely on the discovery — without additional procedures to evaluate the transaction, understand the reason for the omission, and determine whether adequate disclosure can now be made — is premature. The auditor must complete the investigation before determining the effect on the opinion.
explanations.d: The materiality of the transaction is not established by the fact that it was discovered in a single transaction. If the transaction is material, the discovery of an undisclosed related party requires investigation regardless of where it was found.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response
questions.keyword: related parties and related party transactions
questions.text: An entity sold its headquarters building to a newly formed LLC for $12 million. The LLC is managed by the entity's CFO's brother-in-law, who holds a 30% interest; the remaining 70% is held by an offshore trust whose beneficial owner is undisclosed. Management characterized the transaction as arm's-length and did not disclose a related-party relationship. The auditor identifies the CFO's brother-in-law's involvement through a public records search. How should the auditor evaluate this situation?

answers.text: Accept management's characterization since the CFO's brother-in-law is not a direct family member and therefore not a related party under GAAP
Confirm the $12 million price with the LLC's bank to verify receipt of funds, then conclude the transaction was properly recorded

Treat this as a significant finding — the undisclosed relationship involving a family affiliate of a key executive, the opaque ownership structure of the LLC, the affirmative mischaracterization as arm's-length, and the potential for the CFO to benefit indirectly all constitute serious red flags requiring expanded procedures, fraud risk reassessment, and likely communication to those charged with governance
Accept the transaction since real estate transactions are routinely conducted through LLCs and the CFO's brother-in-law is only a minority owner with 30%

explanations.a: Related parties under GAAP (ASC 850) include immediate family members of principal owners and management — and the definition of 'immediate family' and 'affiliated entities' is broad. The CFO's brother-in-law may qualify as a related party depending on the entity's disclosure framework, and regardless of the precise technical definition, the auditor must evaluate whether the relationship could have influenced the transaction terms.
explanations.b: Confirming receipt of funds only verifies the cash receipt — it does not address whether $12 million represents fair market value, whether the transaction was arm's-length, or whether the CFO may have an undisclosed economic interest through the opaque offshore trust structure.
explanations.c: This situation presents multiple compounding red flags that warrant serious professional scrutiny: (1) the CFO's brother-in-law's involvement creates a potential conflict of interest; (2) the undisclosed 70% offshore trust with unknown beneficial owners raises the possibility that the CFO has an indirect economic interest in the transaction; (3) management's affirmative characterization of the transaction as arm's-length — rather than disclosing the potential relationship — suggests intentional concealment; (4) real estate sales of this size to entities with opaque ownership are a common vehicle for fraudulent related-party transactions. The auditor must: investigate the beneficial ownership of the offshore trust (through inquiry, public records, legal engagement); obtain an independent appraisal of the property to evaluate the fairness of the $12 million price; reassess fraud risk given management's apparent concealment; and communicate the findings to the audit committee (bypassing the CFO if the CFO is implicated).
explanations.d: A 30% minority interest is still a significant economic interest — particularly if the CFO has additional interests through the undisclosed offshore trust. The minority percentage alone does not eliminate the related-party concern, particularly given the overall pattern of indicators in this scenario.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response
questions.text: In a single audit, the primary compliance audit objective for each major federal program is to

answers.text: Provide assurance on whether the entity complied with the types of compliance requirements applicable to each major program — such as allowable costs, eligibility, and reporting requirements
Express an opinion on the financial statements of each federal program separately
Certify that all federal grant funds were spent efficiently and that the programs achieved their intended policy outcomes
Test 100% of transactions within each major program to detect all instances of noncompliance

explanations.a: The single audit's compliance audit objective (per 2 CFR 200.514 and AU-C 935) is to provide assurance on whether the non-federal entity complied with the applicable types of compliance requirements for each major program. The Uniform Guidance's Compliance Supplement identifies 12 types of compliance requirements (including activities allowed or unallowed, allowable costs, eligibility, equipment, matching, period of performance, procurement, program income, reporting, subrecipient monitoring, and special tests) that define what the entity must comply with for each program.
explanations.b: The single audit does not express separate financial statement opinions for each federal program. The compliance audit reports on compliance — not on separately presented program financial statements. The entity's overall financial statements receive the standard financial statement opinion.
explanations.c: Program effectiveness and efficiency (whether federal programs achieved their intended outcomes) is evaluated through performance audits — a separate type of engagement. Single audits focus on compliance with federal requirements, not on policy outcomes or program effectiveness.
explanations.d: Single audits use a risk-based sampling approach — not 100% transaction testing. The auditor selects samples based on risk assessment, the nature of the compliance requirements, and the effectiveness of internal controls over compliance. Testing 100% of all transactions in every major program would be impractical and is not required.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response
questions.text: The 2 CFR 200 Compliance Supplement assists auditors in planning single audit procedures primarily by

answers.text: Specifying the exact sample size the auditor must use for each compliance requirement in each federal program
Providing a complete listing of all fraudulent activities detected in federal programs in prior years
Establishing the financial statement materiality threshold for all non-federal entities receiving federal awards

Identifying the applicable types of compliance requirements for specific federal programs, the compliance requirements most likely to result in material noncompliance, and the suggested audit procedures to test compliance

explanations.a: The Compliance Supplement does not specify exact sample sizes — sample size determination is a professional judgment based on risk, the nature of the compliance requirement, and the effectiveness of internal controls. The Supplement provides guidance on what to test, not precisely how large the sample must be.
explanations.b: The Compliance Supplement is not a database of prior detected fraud — it is a guidance document developed by the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) that describes federal programs and their compliance requirements. It is prospective planning guidance, not historical fraud data.
explanations.c: The Compliance Supplement does not establish financial statement materiality thresholds for single audit entities. Materiality for the financial statement audit is determined by the auditor using professional judgment, and compliance materiality for each program is separately determined by the auditor for the compliance audit.
explanations.d: The 2 CFR 200 Compliance Supplement is published annually by OMB and is the primary planning tool for single audit compliance testing. For each significant federal program, it provides: the applicable types of compliance requirements (which of the 12 types apply to that program); the program-specific compliance requirements that are most likely to have material noncompliance; and suggested audit procedures for testing compliance. Auditors use the Supplement to tailor their compliance testing to the specific requirements of each major program rather than testing all 12 types for every program.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response
questions.text: In planning a single audit, how does the auditor assess the risk of material noncompliance for a major federal program?

answers.text: The auditor applies the same risk assessment as used for the financial statement audit — there is no separate risk assessment for compliance

The auditor assesses the risk of material noncompliance for each applicable compliance requirement in each major program — considering factors such as the nature of the requirement, the entity's history of compliance findings, the complexity of requirements, and the effectiveness of internal controls over compliance
Risk of material noncompliance is presumed to be low for all Type A programs since they have been identified as major programs through the risk-based selection process
The auditor does not assess risk for individual compliance requirements — the assessment is made only at the program level, not at the requirement level

explanations.a: The financial statement audit risk assessment and the compliance audit risk assessment are distinct — while they share the same entity context, they address different objectives. The financial statement audit assesses the risk of material misstatement in the financial statements; the compliance audit assesses the risk of material noncompliance with applicable federal requirements for each major program. The risk factors, procedures, and conclusions are separate.
