explanations.b: For each major program and applicable compliance requirement, the auditor performs a risk assessment that considers: (1) the nature of the compliance requirement — some requirements (eligibility, allowable costs) are inherently more complex and judgment-intensive; (2) the entity's prior compliance history — prior findings or questioned costs in specific programs indicate elevated risk; (3) the complexity of the requirement and associated regulations; (4) the adequacy of internal controls over compliance (ICoc) — strong controls reduce the risk of noncompliance going undetected; and (5) any risk factors identified by the Compliance Supplement for that program. This assessment drives the nature and extent of compliance testing.
explanations.c: Type A programs are required to be audited as major programs (unless low-risk), but that designation does not reduce the compliance risk assessment within those programs. Being audited as major means the program receives the required compliance testing — the level of risk within the program still must be assessed to design appropriate procedures.
explanations.d: Risk assessment for compliance is performed at the compliance requirement level within each major program — not just at the program level. Different requirements within the same program may have very different risk levels — for example, eligibility requirements may be high-risk while reporting requirements may be lower risk for the same program.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response
questions.text: In a single audit, internal control over compliance (ICoc) differs from internal control over financial reporting (ICFR) primarily because

answers.text: ICoc is evaluated only by the entity's management, not by the external auditor
ICFR covers all controls in the entity, while ICoc covers only controls over payroll and procurement

ICoc addresses whether the entity has controls that provide reasonable assurance of compliance with the applicable federal program requirements — a separate objective from the financial reporting accuracy addressed by ICFR
ICoc and ICFR are identical — a single evaluation satisfies both requirements in a single audit

explanations.a: The external auditor evaluates ICoc as part of the single audit — not management alone. The auditor obtains an understanding of ICoc for each major program and, as part of the compliance audit, assesses the design and implementation of relevant controls (and tests operating effectiveness when the auditor intends to rely on them to reduce compliance testing).
explanations.b: ICFR covers controls over the financial reporting process broadly — not limited to specific processes. ICoc covers controls specific to compliance with federal program requirements, which may include controls over eligibility verification, cost allocation, subrecipient monitoring, and reporting — processes that may overlap with ICFR but are evaluated from a compliance perspective.
explanations.c: ICoc and ICFR have distinct objectives. ICFR addresses whether controls provide reasonable assurance that financial transactions are recorded accurately in accordance with GAAP. ICoc addresses whether controls provide reasonable assurance that the entity is complying with the federal laws, regulations, and grant terms applicable to each major program. While there is some overlap (e.g., controls over recording grant expenditures affect both ICFR and ICoc), the objectives, criteria, and audit procedures are fundamentally different. A deficiency in ICoc — such as the absence of eligibility verification procedures — may not affect ICFR at all.
explanations.d: ICoc and ICFR evaluations are conducted separately using different criteria. A single evaluation cannot satisfy both. The financial statement audit addresses ICFR through risk assessment and testing; the compliance audit addresses ICoc through a separate understanding of controls relevant to each major program's compliance requirements.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Assessing Risk and Developing a Planned Response
questions.text: A non-federal entity has received single audits for five consecutive years. In four of those years, it received unmodified opinions on both financial statements and compliance, with no material weaknesses in ICFR or ICoc, and submitted its single audit reporting packages to the Federal Audit Clearinghouse on time. In the current year, the entity received an unmodified financial statement opinion but has a material weakness in ICoc related to its eligibility verification process. Which assessment of its low-risk auditee status for the FOLLOWING year is MOST accurate?

answers.text: The entity will qualify as a low-risk auditee in the following year because it has four consecutive years of clean audits and the current-year material weakness is in compliance, not financial reporting
The entity will qualify as a low-risk auditee in the following year because the material weakness is in ICoc rather than ICFR — only ICFR weaknesses disqualify an entity from low-risk auditee status

The entity will not qualify as a low-risk auditee in the following year because the current-year material weakness in ICoc disqualifies it — the low-risk criteria require no material weaknesses in ICFR or compliance-related controls for the prior two years
The entity automatically qualifies as low-risk after five consecutive single audits regardless of the content of those audits

explanations.a: This overestimates the entity's qualification prospects. The Uniform Guidance low-risk auditee criteria (2 CFR § 200.520) require that for both of the prior two years: the financial statement audit opinion was unmodified; the single audit report on compliance was unmodified (no material instances of noncompliance); there were no material weaknesses in ICFR or internal control over compliance; and the reporting package was submitted on time. A material weakness in ICoc in the current year — even if ICFR is clean — would fail the low-risk criteria for the following year.
explanations.b: The Uniform Guidance's low-risk auditee criteria require no material weaknesses in both ICFR AND compliance-related controls. The criteria do not distinguish between types of material weaknesses — a material weakness in ICoc is just as disqualifying as one in ICFR.
explanations.c: Under 2 CFR § 200.520, low-risk auditee status is available to entities that meet all qualifying criteria for the two most recent single audit periods. The criteria include: unmodified opinions on financial statements and compliance; no material weaknesses in ICFR or internal control over compliance; and timely submission. A material weakness in ICoc in the current year means the entity fails the qualification criteria for the following year — regardless of its strong track record in prior years. Low-risk status must be earned each year based on the current and prior year's performance.
explanations.d: The number of consecutive single audits does not automatically confer low-risk status. Low-risk auditee status is a risk-based classification that must be earned based on specific performance criteria for the two most recent audits — not simply by having a long history of being audited.
